pages.title: How should ACT pitch Minderoo in line with its current strategy, and what money framing fits best?
pages.excerpt: Synthesised from the wiki on 2026-04-21. This article was generated by a query and saved back into Tractorpedia so the next question can build on top of it.
pages.content:
> Synthesised from the wiki on 2026-04-21. This article was generated by a query and saved back into Tractorpedia so the next question can build on top of it.

## Answer

## Short answer

The strongest Minderoo pitch is **not** "fund JusticeHub" and it is **not** "fund the library" and it is definitely not "fund an AI platform."

The strongest pitch is: **fund a place-based, ACCO-led early-intervention infrastructure that bends a late-intervention cost curve Minderoo already publicly owns.**

As of **21 April 2026**, this is the closest fit to Minderoo's current public strategy based on their official [Communities page](https://www.minderoo.org/communities/), [2030 Strategy PDF](https://cdn.minderoo.org/assets/new/documents/Minderoo-Foundation-Strategy.pdf), [Cost of Late Intervention media release from 27 August 2025](https://www.minderoo.org/media/australia-s-spiraling-cost-of-missing-early-warning-signs-in-our-children/), [Nicola Forrest's statement from 27 August 2025](https://www.minderoo.org/media/every-child-no-matter-their-postcode-deserves-the-best-start-in-life/), and the [2025 Impact Report](https://report.minderoo.org/).

## What Minderoo is actually telling us it wants

Minderoo's current Communities focus area is explicit about five things:

- all children reaching their full potential in thriving communities
- local knowledge and lived experience
- place-based engagement
- stronger child and family support ecosystems
- vibrant, connected communities

Its 2025 impact language is also explicit about the four roles it plays: **Partner, Develop, Advocate, Generate Evidence**.

That means ACT should pitch The Three Circles as a program that lets Minderoo do all four roles at once:

- **Partner** with 5 confirmed ACCO anchors and 2-3 more co-selected with community consent
- **Develop** a transferable place-based method across those anchors, the Judges on Country loop, and the Brave Ones practice
- **Generate evidence** through JusticeHub, CivicGraph, Empathy Ledger, and the live anchor dataset
- **Advocate** through the national artefact, magistrate-facing tools, and policy visibility that follows from them

This is a much cleaner fit than leading with product, design, or art.

## The most meaningful oar

The most meaningful oar is **not Circle One** and it is **not Circle Three**.

It is **Circle Two: the relational hold inside the anchor communities.**

Why:

1. It maps directly to Minderoo's **Place-based Engagement** body of work.
2. It is where the Communities strategy is strongest: local knowledge, lived experience, community power, vibrant connected places.
3. It lets ACT translate youth justice into an **early-intervention** story instead of a detention-response story.
4. It makes the rest of the stack make sense. JusticeHub becomes the evidence layer underneath the anchor work. The Brave Ones becomes the qualitative trace layer and human proof. The library becomes the advocacy artefact at the end, not the thing being bought at the start.

If ACT is asked what the program really is in one sentence, the cleanest answer is:

**A three-year partnership to hold community-led alternatives long enough for them to bend the child-protection-to-youth-justice trajectory, prove what works, and make it visible nationally.**

That is much closer to Minderoo's official language than "a national justice platform" or "an art-and-data library."

## The decisive wedge: child protection to youth justice

The strongest strategic wedge is not detention by itself. It is the transition from **child protection into youth justice**.

Minderoo's COLI framing makes this powerful because their own public material says:

- late intervention costs **$22.3B annually**
- that figure is up **47% since 2019**
- child protection is the largest line item
- youth crime is the second-largest line item
- acting earlier is about "spending smarter," not merely spending more

So ACT should make one move very clearly:

**We are upstream of the point where child protection becomes youth justice.**

That turns the pitch from a justice special case into a Communities portfolio bridge:

- early-years logic
- wrap-around supports
- family and community environment
- later youth-justice consequences

That bridge is what makes Lucy's internal case easier.

## What to lead with, in order

### 1. Start with Communities, not JusticeHub

Open with the five ACCO anchors and the place-based method. JusticeHub is not the opening noun. It is the evidence infrastructure under the method.

### 2. Use Minderoo's own portfolio grammar

The cleanest order is:

- **Place-based engagement**: five confirmed anchors, two to three more co-selected
- **Improving child and family supports**: wrap-around community hold, not fragmented services
- **Generate evidence**: the live map, service legibility, anchor data, storyteller corpus
- **Advocate**: judges, magistrates, national artefact, public proof

### 3. Use The Brave Ones as proof, not as the main ask

The Brave Ones matters because it carries the human trace layer that makes the system memorable and honest. But it should not be the top-line reason for the grant.

### 4. Make the library the destination, not the starting price tag

The library is a strong conceptual hook. It is not the first budget category Lucy should have to defend internally.

## The best money framing

### Recommended primary ask

**Lead with the canonical `Three Circles` ask: $2.9M over 3 years.**

Why this is the best fit:

- it is already the canonical ask in [[three-circles|The Three Circles]]
- it is sized as a real **multi-year partnership**, which fits Minderoo's 2025 "Pay What It Takes" posture and three-year budget language
- it is big enough to fund the actual place-based hold, evidence layer, and national translation
- it does not overweight the artefact and publishing layer the way the older $3.43M Crescendo package does
- it is easier to defend as a Communities investment than a larger, more library-forward number

### Recommended entry point

If Minderoo needs a staged internal decision, the best on-ramp is:

**$780K for Year 1, with right-of-first-refusal or indicative hold on Years 2-3.**

This is already the clean internal gate in the campaign brief and the canonical page. It gives Minderoo a credible Year 1 commitment without forcing ACT into a one-year-only posture.

### Recommended external budget story

Narrate the $2.9M in Minderoo's role language, not ACT's internal production language:

- **Partner / place-based hold:** $1.4M
  This is the anchor communities, domestic exchanges, and relational infrastructure.
- **Generate evidence:** $0.8M
  This is the living map, JusticeHub, Empathy Ledger, CivicGraph integration, and the measure/learn layer.
- **Develop + Advocate:** $0.7M
  This is Judges on Country, national artefacts, documentary/book/platform release, and policy translation.

This is cleaner for Lucy than opening with line items like journals, printing, or media production.

## What not to do with the money story

### Do not lead with $3.43M

The older `minderoo-pitch-package` framing defaults to **Crescendo = $3.43M / 3 years**. That is still useful as a stretch or expanded version, but it is not the best opening number if the goal is clean strategy fit.

The problem is not that $3.43M is impossible. The problem is that it foregrounds the library and production envelope too early, which makes the ask feel more like a large cultural product build than a place-based Communities investment.

### Do not lead with the single-circle infrastructure ask

The `three-circles` page includes a single-circle option. That is useful as a rescue path. It is a weak opening move because it strips out the exact place-based relational work Minderoo is most clearly saying it wants.

### Do not frame the grant as software build

Minderoo's public role language leaves room for evidence and tools, but the Communities strategy is not asking for a speculative platform build. The tech only works in the pitch when it is visibly subordinate to the community hold.

## The practical recommendation

If ACT wants the cleanest, most strategy-native sentence to carry into the next Lucy conversation, it is this:

**We are asking Minderoo to make a three-year Communities investment in 5 confirmed ACCO anchors and 2-3 more co-selected with community consent, with JusticeHub as the evidence layer and The Brave Ones as the human trace layer, to bend the child-protection-to-youth-justice trajectory that Minderoo's own $22.3B late-intervention work has already made undeniable.**

And if Lucy asks the number:

- **Primary answer:** `$2.9M over 3 years`
- **If staged:** `$780K for Year 1, with pathway to the full three-year partnership`
- **Only if invited upward:** `$3.43M` as the expanded Crescendo expression

That is the strongest strategic fit currently available in the repo.

pages.title: Indigenous Data Sovereignty
pages.excerpt: The right of Indigenous peoples to govern the collection, ownership, and application of data about their communities, lands, and cultures.
pages.content:
> The right of Indigenous peoples to govern the collection, ownership, and application of data about their communities, lands, and cultures.

## CARE Principles

The foundational framework, developed by the Global Indigenous Data Alliance (GIDA):

- **Collective benefit** — data ecosystems designed for Indigenous innovation and self-determination
- **Authority to control** — Indigenous peoples' rights to control and govern their data
- **Responsibility** — those working with Indigenous data have a responsibility to nurture respectful relationships
- **Ethics** — Indigenous peoples' rights and wellbeing must be the primary concern

## Mukurtu CMS

**Mukurtu** is a Warumungu word meaning "dilly bag" — a safe keeping place for sacred materials.

Created in 2007 as a grassroots project, Mukurtu supports Indigenous communities worldwide to safeguard cultural knowledge while respecting traditional protocols. Built on **Drupal**, which has recently integrated the **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** — enabling AI agents to securely connect while respecting access controls.

### Why Mukurtu Matters for ACT

- **TK Labels** embedded directly in metadata — restrictions based on gender, seasonal conditions, sacredness
- **Drupal + MCP** = AI agents can query the archive while mathematically obeying cultural protocols
- **Jumbunna Institute (UTS)** partnership for digitizing significant Aboriginal political history
- Perfect fit for [[palm-island|Palm Island]]'s PICC 20-year archive and Empathy Ledger content

### Integration with ACT Stack

Mukurtu provides the **governance layer** for the [[local-ai-architecture|Local AI Architecture]]:
1. Raw cultural materials stored in Mukurtu with TK Labels
2. YAML frontmatter on every markdown file carries protocol metadata
3. AI agents read TK Labels before processing — cannot synthesize restricted content
4. Community retains absolute ownership of both data and intelligence

## Traditional Knowledge (TK) Labels

Digital tags from the [Local Contexts Hub](https://localcontexts.org/) that identify place-based knowledge carrying cultural rights:

- **TK Attribution** — credit to the community
- **TK Non-Commercial** — not for commercial use without consent
- **TK Culturally Sensitive** — contains sensitive material
- **TK Community Voice** — only community can speak to meaning
- **TK Seasonal** — access restricted to certain times
- **TK Men/Women Restricted** — gender-specific protocols

## Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC)

For Empathy Ledger narratives especially — consent must be:
- **Ongoing** (not one-time sign-off)
- **Revocable** (community can withdraw data at any stage)
- **Granular** (different levels for different uses)
- **Culturally appropriate** (consent processes designed with community)

## Key Organizations

| Organization                           | Role                                                           |
| -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Maiam nayri Wingara Collective         | Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islander Data Sovereignty authority |
| Jumbunna Institute (UTS)               | Digitizing Aboriginal political history via Mukurtu            |
| GIDA (Global Indigenous Data Alliance) | International CARE principles framework                        |
| Local Contexts Hub                     | TK and Biocultural Labels system                               |

## Sami Precedent (Sweden)

The Sami people (Sapmi region across Sweden, Norway, Finland) are pushing institutions to adopt CARE principles as a mandatory global standard through the GIDA-Sapmi network. The Sami Parliament's push for data rights demonstrates that sovereign storytelling can be formalized into national policy.

## Backlinks

- [[third-reality|The Third Reality]] — the methodology requiring sovereign data
- [[picc|Palm Island Community Company]] — primary implementation site
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — narrative sovereignty platform
- [[ocap-principles|OCAP Principles]] — rights-based foundation underneath Indigenous data sovereignty practice
- [[consent-as-infrastructure|Consent as Infrastructure]] — concrete consent model that operationalizes sovereignty in product architecture
- [[local-ai-architecture|Local AI Architecture]] — technical implementation
- [[global-precedents|Global Precedents]] — Sweden, Spain, Holland examples
- [[transcript-analysis-method|Transcript Analysis Method]] — one concrete pipeline where sovereignty constraints shape AI use, review, and publication

pages.title: Industry Residency at The Harvest
pages.excerpt: We host industry residencies at The Harvest — extended placements where artists, designers and ACT work alongside a regional industry and its people. Not an artist-in-residence at a company. A community treating its own industry, land and elders as the material, with us holding the studio.
pages.content:
> We host industry residencies at [[the-harvest|The Harvest]] — extended placements where artists, designers and ACT work alongside a regional industry and its people. Not an artist-in-residence at a company. A community treating its own industry, land and elders as the material, with us holding the studio.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-FM-EXP-industry-residency-at-the-harvest | **Cluster:** [[act-farm|ACT Farm]]

## What it is

An industry residency is not an artist residency. We run both at ACT — the [[experiences/artist-residency|Artist Residency at BCV]] places an artist on Country and the land is the commission. An industry residency at [[the-harvest|The Harvest]] starts from the other end: a regional industry, its producers, processors, elders, its disappearing knowledge. Artists and designers come in alongside ACT to build the artefacts, structures and conversations that make the industry visible to itself.

Where the artist residency asks *what can an artist make here*, the industry residency asks *what does this industry want to see of itself, and who needs to be in the room for that to happen*.

We run this out of The Harvest — the former Green Harvest site in Witta, Kabi Kabi and Jinibara Country — because the site has the ground, the standing infrastructure, the kitchen, and the public-facing hours that this kind of work needs. [[case-studies/radical-scoops-at-the-harvest|Radical Scoops]] — our second-project selection in Regional Arts Australia's Industry Residencies Pilot — is the proof this works.

## Who it's for

- **Regional industries** that want to understand themselves through creative practice rather than consultancy decks — agriculture, timber, dairy, hospitality, fibre, fisheries
- **Arts-and-industry funding programs** — Regional Arts Australia, ANAT, Creative Australia, state arts bodies, regional arts development funds
- **Artists and designers** whose practice sits at the intersection of material, industry, community, and documentation
- **Philanthropic partners** looking for a placed, durable way into regional economic resilience
- **Communities** that want to commission work about their own unspoken histories — elders, industries, land changes, knowledge layers that were never asked about

We're not the right fit for activations, brand residencies, or short-form "artists visit industry" programs. An industry residency here is measured in months to years, not weeks.

## What happens

Each residency is shaped to its industry and community, but the backbone is shared:

- **A leased footprint.** We anchor the residency on a physical site at The Harvest — studio, workshop, pop-up spaces — held for the duration so the work can settle.
- **An industry proposition.** We identify the local industry, its producers, its unspoken knowledge, and the communities connected through it. This is not abstract — it's the dairy farmer across the road, the oyster farmer up the coast, the timber cutter who worked the region sixty years ago.
- **A circular-economy brief.** Every structure, every artefact, every output is designed with its next life specified. Temporary buildings become beds or housing for remote communities. Shells become paths. Non-permanence is a design constraint, not a slogan.
- **A documentation discipline.** Photography, audio, writing, [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] story capture — with consent — runs from day one. The residency produces a knowledge layer alongside the physical work.
- **Public-facing pop-ups and convenings** that bring the industry and community into the same room over the residency's duration, rather than staging a single exhibition at the end.
- **An adjacent capacity phase.** The residency funds delivery. We apply in parallel for capacity funding (governance, digital systems, volunteer pathways, replication toolkit) so the model doesn't end when the program money ends. This is how a one-site residency becomes a pattern other regions can adapt.

## Price, duration, capacity

| Item | Detail |
|------|--------|
| **Duration** | 6–12 months on site minimum; Capacity Lab follow-on typically 12 months |
| **Capacity** | One industry proposition at a time per site; multiple artists/collaborators embedded |
| **Funding model** | Primarily grant-funded (RAA Industry Residencies, ANAT, state arts bodies, philanthropic partners); co-contributions from industry and community welcomed |
| **Cost structure** | Tiered — fully funded placements through program partners; co-designed with philanthropic or industry partners; ACT does not run a published rack rate |
| **Includes** | Site access at The Harvest, ACT co-production and governance, documentation discipline, ecosystem integration with [[black-cockatoo-valley|BCV]] and [[experiences/harvest-pairings|Harvest Pairings]] |
| **Doesn't include** | Artist fees (budgeted per residency), industry-partner time, participant travel |
| **Season** | Year-round, with seasonality baked into the program design (food, harvest cycles, industry rhythms) |

Pricing is genuinely per-residency. Bring a funded program, or come to us with an industry and a question; we'll help design the funding case.

## Ecosystem links

- [[the-harvest|The Harvest]] — the Witta site, the kitchen, the public hours
- [[black-cockatoo-valley|Black Cockatoo Valley]] — the residential and convening layer when the residency needs one
- [[experiences/harvest-pairings|Harvest Pairings]] — the day-to-day cross-site pattern this residency thickens
- [[experiences/artist-residency|Artist Residency at BCV]] — the sibling (but distinct) residency shape
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — the documentation and story-return pathway

## Related case studies

- [[case-studies/radical-scoops-at-the-harvest|Radical Scoops at The Harvest — the RAA Industry Residency]] — the live instance. 12-month lease, about 1,000 milk crates, ice cream as connective tissue, Barry's red-cedar story, pop-up deli, Capacity Lab phase in design.

## How to inquire

By conversation, not application round. Tell us the industry you want to work with, the community or place it connects to, the funding context you're working inside (or need help to build), and the artists or practitioners you'd want embedded. We reply within a few working days and usually run two or three calls before any proposal is drafted. Inquiries go through `/experiences/industry-residency-at-the-harvest` on the ACT Farm site.

## LCAA Phase

In the [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]], an Industry Residency at The Harvest extends the method across months and years — Listen → Curiosity → Action → Art applied to a regional industry rather than an artist's question. Here's how the four phases show up:

- **Listen** — to the local industry, its producers, processors, elders, and the disappearing knowledge layer; conversations with the dairy farmer across the road, the oyster farmer up the coast, the timber cutter who worked the region sixty years ago
- **Curiosity** — what does this industry want to see of itself, and who needs to be in the room for that to happen? An industry proposition co-shaped with community
- **Action** — leased footprint at The Harvest; circular-economy brief where every structure has its next life specified; documentation discipline running from day one; public-facing pop-ups and convenings rather than a single closing exhibition
- **Art** — the artefacts and structures the residency produces; the knowledge layer captured through [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]]; the Capacity Lab follow-on that turns a one-site residency into a pattern other regions can adapt

Where the [[experiences/artist-residency|artist residency]] asks *what can an artist make here*, the industry residency asks *what does this industry want to see of itself, and who needs to be in the room for that to happen*. [[case-studies/radical-scoops-at-the-harvest|Radical Scoops]] is the live instance.

pages.content:
> We run focused one- to two-day innovation sessions across four practice areas — youth justice, AI and systems, data and evidence, storytelling. Small rooms, real problems, no theatre.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-FM-EXP-innovation-sessions | **Cluster:** [[act-farm|ACT Farm]]

## What it is

Innovation Sessions are ACT-led working sessions around a specific problem a partner is trying to move. They're not strategy workshops in the generic sense and they're not innovation-theatre with post-its. We bring ACT's method, our ecosystem knowledge, and — when it helps — the right people from our network.

We run four distinct tracks:

### Youth justice
Sessions for organisations working inside or adjacent to the youth justice system — diversion programs, aftercare, family services, education-justice crossovers. We bring the [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] frame, [[custodian-economy|Custodian Economy]] thinking, and the lessons from on-Country work.

### AI and systems
Sessions for organisations grappling with AI as infrastructure — not as product. Includes LLM trust boundaries, consent-first data, [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] patterns, and the [[civicgraph|CivicGraph]] lens on sector-scale systems.

### Data and evidence
Sessions on evidence infrastructure — how to make the data legible to funders, communities, and regulators without flattening it. Covers [[consent-as-infrastructure|consent]], measurement, and how evidence becomes relational rather than extractive.

### Storytelling
Sessions on [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] method at program scale — consent, cultural sensitivity, elder approval, return-to-community publishing. Pairs naturally with the [[experiences/empathy-ledger-storytelling-residency|storytelling residency]].

## Who it's for

- Community-sector leadership teams with a specific, namable problem
- Funders wanting a working session rather than a pitch meeting
- Government and agency teams commissioning community-facing programs
- ACT partners needing a focused day on one of the four tracks

## What happens

One- or two-day intensive, usually 6–15 people in the room.

- Pre-session: a short brief back from us on how we'd frame the problem
- Day: short inputs, longer working blocks, honest conversation, decisions
- Post-session: a written note of decisions and next steps — not a deck

Can run at BCV, in your office, or hybrid. The format is the product, not the venue.

## Price, duration, capacity

| Item | Detail |
|------|--------|
| **Duration** | 1–2 days |
| **Capacity** | 6–15 |
| **Price** | Day-rate per facilitator, plus materials and venue if at BCV. Community-sector rate available |
| **Includes** | Design, facilitation, post-session note |

pages.title: Jesús Teruel — Diagrama Key Story
pages.excerpt: A respect-centred approach to youth rehabilitation and reintegration that offers a live reference for humane justice practice.
pages.content:
> A respect-centred approach to youth rehabilitation and reintegration that offers a live reference for humane justice practice.

## Context

**Place:** Murcia, Spain (Diagrama Foundation)
**Voice Owner:** Diagrama practice leader
**Consent Status:** EXTERNAL-LITE

## Story

Jesús Teruel's work with the Diagrama Foundation in Spain offers something rare: a live, operating example of youth justice done differently. While Australian conversations about youth justice often get stuck between punishment and permissiveness, Diagrama demonstrates a third way.

The approach centres on respect — for young people, for their potential, for their complexity. Key principles:
- Young people are treated as capable of change
- Relationships with staff are primary tools
- Environment matters — design for dignity
- Integration into community is the goal from day one
- Measurement focuses on wellbeing, not just compliance

ACT's learning journey to Diagrama wasn't about importing a model. It was about seeing proof that alternatives work, and bringing that evidence into Australian conversations.

pages.title: Judges on Country
pages.excerpt: "Our young people don't experience your decisions as process. They experience them as consequences."
pages.content:
> "Our young people don't experience your decisions as process. They experience them as consequences."

**Status:** Active | **Cluster:** [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] | **Location:** Mparntwe (Alice Springs)

## Overview

Judges on Country is not a workshop. Not training. Not a conference breakout session with takeaway slides. It is a controlled moment of moral uncertainty inside a judge's own professional role — 30 minutes that change the way 55 judges from across Australia understand what happens after they hand down a decision.

The program brings judges to Mparntwe to learn from Traditional Owners about Indigenous history, youth justice, and what it means for young people who move through the system. It is led by Traditional Owners — Kristy Bloomfield and Tanya Turner from [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] — and by Oonchiumpa itself as a program.

The premise is simple and uncomfortable: the people sentencing these children have never met one outside the dock.

## The numbers that frame the room

Before any experience begins, the numbers need to be in the room:

- **$1.3M+ per year** to detain one child in Australia
- **80%+ reoffending rate** from detention — the system produces the thing it claims to prevent
- **60%+ of detained youth are Indigenous** — in a country where Indigenous people are 3% of the population
- **[[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]]: 95% diversion rate, 97.6% less cost** than detention
- **Operation Luna:** 20 of 21 high-risk youth removed from the list through community-led intervention

These are not arguments. They are the baseline. The experience design puts a human face on the gap between those numbers and what a judge actually knows when they decide.

## The experience design (30 minutes)

This is the core of the program. Every element is deliberate. The pacing is tight. The discomfort is the point.

### 0-5 min — Grounding

Led by Traditional Owners. Not a welcome speech. Not an acknowledgement of country read from a card. Direct:

*"Our young people don't experience your decisions as process. They experience them as consequences."*

The room is oriented. The judges are not here as guests being hosted. They are here as decision-makers being confronted — respectfully, but without ambiguity — with what their decisions produce.

### 5-10 min — Meet the person

Each judge receives a physical card. A photo. A name. An age. A moment. A quote. Just enough — like a court file snapshot, except this time the file has a face looking back.

These are Story Cards from [[#the-card-deck|the card deck]]. The portraits come from [[the-brave-ones|The Brave Ones]] — Phase 1 pilot portraits become the faces judges hold in their hands.

No context about offence history. No risk assessment. No system language. Just a young person.

### 10-15 min — Decide

*"You don't get more time. This is what court feels like. Decide."*

Three lenses are presented on a Decision Point Card:

1. **Offence-first** — what did they do?
2. **Risk-first** — what might they do?
3. **Person-and-context-first** — who are they, where are they, what do they need?

Each judge chooses individually. No discussion. No group consensus. They sit with their decision the way a young person sits with theirs.

### 15-20 min — Undo their certainty

New information arrives. One piece at a time. Pause between each.

*"He hasn't been home in 3 weeks."*

*"There is no transport to the nearest program."*

*"This is his third breach, not third offence."*

Then the question:

*"Would you make the same decision now?"*

The information they didn't have is the information the system routinely doesn't provide. The gap is not an accident. It is structural.

### 20-25 min — The uncomfortable truth

Traditional Owners step back in. Kristy Bloomfield. Tanya Turner. The people who hold the young people after the decision is made.

*"You are asked to decide quickly. Without knowing what matters. And then they live with that decision for years."*

This is not accusation. It is description. The system's design is the problem, not the individual judge's intent. But the individual judge is the one who signs the order.

### 25-28 min — Show the alternative

A real local program. Or the absence of one. Pathway Cards show what happens next under each decision — standard pathway versus supported pathway. Program/Place Cards show what actually exists in the young person's community.

This is where [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] becomes real. Not as a platform pitch. As the answer to the question every judge in the room is now asking: *"What can I actually do differently tomorrow?"*

Every QR code on every card opens JusticeHub — filtered to that region, showing real programs, eligibility, who to contact. The alternative exists. But only if you know it's there.

### 28-30 min — Leave them unsettled

Final words from community:

*"We are not asking you to fix everything. But next time you see a young person like this, know that what you don't know matters."*

No neat ending. No resolution. No action items or feedback forms. The discomfort is the deliverable. A judge who leaves this room certain has missed the point.

## The card deck

Four card types, physically printed. Designed to be held, turned over, kept. Not slides. Not PDFs. Objects that stay in a judge's chambers.

### 1. Story Cards

Photo on one side. On the reverse: a quote, 2-3 lines. The person, not the file.

The portraits are from [[the-brave-ones|The Brave Ones]]. The connection is direct: the same visual discipline — high-contrast B&W, devotional close framing, the dignity register — that the counter-mugshot series uses for galleries and exhibitions is what a judge holds in their hand at the moment of decision.

### 2. Decision Point Cards

*"Which lens is guiding your next step?"*

- Offence-first
- Risk-first
- Relationship-and-context-first
- Explore alternatives

No right answer is marked. The card forces the judge to name their frame, not hide behind "standard procedure."

### 3. Pathway Cards

What happens next under each choice. Two columns: standard pathway versus supported pathway. The divergence is stark. One column ends in a cycle. The other ends in a person with a plan.

### 4. Program/Place Cards

Real alternatives. The physical card carries a short summary — program name, location, what it does, who it's for. The QR code on each card opens the live [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] entry for that program: current availability, eligibility criteria, contact details, community context.

These cards are the bridge between the experience and the platform. The moment in the room becomes a tool in the courtroom.

## Connection to The Brave Ones

The portraits ARE the Story Cards. [[the-brave-ones|The Brave Ones]] Phase 1 pilot portraits — the first five young people photographed in Mparntwe, Bourke, and one other community — become the faces judges hold in their hands during the experience.

This is the design loop: portraits shot with [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] consent, printed as Story Cards for Judges on Country, exhibited as gallery pieces in [[contained|CONTAINED]] rooms, published as JusticeHub nodes. One sitting, four surfaces, every one consent-governed.

## Connection to JusticeHub

Every QR on every card opens [[justicehub|JusticeHub]]. The platform answers the question the experience creates: *"What can I actually do differently tomorrow?"*

JusticeHub filtered to a region shows real programs, real eligibility, real contact details. It shows where the system works and where it doesn't. It shows gaps — places where the only option is detention because no alternative has been funded.

The card deck makes JusticeHub tangible. The platform makes the card deck actionable.

## Connection to Empathy Ledger

The six postcard stories from the Mparntwe community — Kristy and Tanya together, Jackquann and Nigel together, Jackquann alone, Nigel alone, Laquisha, and Fred with Xavier — syndicate as [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] articles at `/stories/empathy-ledger/{slug}`.

These are not promotional materials. They are first-person accounts held in the consent layer, surfaced where they are needed: in a judge's hand, on a gallery wall, in a JusticeHub profile, in a funder deck. Same story, same consent, different surface.

## Connection to Three Circles and Staying

Judges on Country operationalises the [[three-circles|Three Circles]] methodology at the judicial education layer. The experience design follows Listen (grounding, meet the person), Curiosity (decide, undo certainty), Action (show the alternative), and the card deck is the Art — the artefact that persists after the moment.

The [[staying|Staying]] methodology matters here because the card deck is not a one-off conference handout. The Program/Place Cards update as JusticeHub updates. The Story Cards grow as [[the-brave-ones|The Brave Ones]] cohort grows. The experience is designed to be repeated — new judges, new cohorts, new communities — because the team stays.

## Cultural protocol

All cultural protocol for Judges on Country follows the same non-negotiable framework as [[the-brave-ones|The Brave Ones]]:

1. **Kristy Bloomfield and Tanya Turner** at [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] co-design the experience and lead it. This is not a guest appearance. They are the authority in the room.
2. **No young person's story is used without [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] consent** — including right of withdrawal at any point
3. **Story Cards featuring subjects under 18** require guardian and cultural authority sign-off
4. **Traditional Owners are compensated** as the expert facilitators they are, not as cultural consultants on a day rate
5. **The experience does not happen without community leadership present** — if Kristy and Tanya are not available, the session does not run with substitutes

## LCAA Phase

In the [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]], Judges on Country sits in the **Action** phase — it is a controlled moment of moral uncertainty inside a judge's own professional role, designed to change the way 55 judges from across Australia understand what happens after they hand down a decision. The card deck is the persistent **Art** that follows the experience back into chambers.

LCAA arc for Judges on Country:
- **Listen** — Traditional Owners ([[kristy-bloomfield|Kristy Bloomfield]] and Tanya Turner from [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]]) lead the Grounding (0–5 min); a Story Card carrying a young person's photo, name, age, and quote — *"like a court file snapshot, except this time the file has a face looking back"*
- **Curiosity** — three lenses on the Decision Point Card (offence-first, risk-first, person-and-context-first); new information arriving one piece at a time after the decision is made — *"would you make the same decision now?"*
- **Action** — Pathway Cards showing what happens next under each choice (standard pathway versus supported pathway); Program/Place Cards opening live [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] entries via QR code, filtered to the young person's region — the alternative exists, but only if you know it's there
- **Art** — the card deck itself as the persistent artefact; portraits drawn from [[the-brave-ones|The Brave Ones]] discipline; the discomfort as the deliverable — *"a judge who leaves this room certain has missed the point"*

Judges on Country operationalises the [[three-circles|Three Circles]] methodology at the judicial education layer, with [[staying|Staying]] as the discipline that keeps it from being a one-off conference handout.

## Connected Stories

Twenty-two stories from the Mparntwe community are held in the wiki. These are the evidence base for Judges on Country — what judges read before, during, and after the experience.

### Postcard Stories (the 6 cards)

The physical cards judges hold in their hands. Each one is a first-person account from the community.

- [[stories/oonchiumpa-kristy-tanya-founders|Kristy & Tanya — "Our young people are just collateral"]]
- [[stories/oonchiumpa-jackquann-nigel-programs|Jackquann & Nigel — "Programs." "Go to school every day."]]
- [[stories/oonchiumpa-jackquann-detention|Jackquann — "Detention. That's not my home."]]
- [[stories/oonchiumpa-nigel-court|Nigel — "When I'm talking to the judge, I feel like I'm panicking."]]
- [[stories/oonchiumpa-laquisha-darwin|Laquisha — "Court is scary because you don't know whether you're getting out or not."]]
- [[stories/oonchiumpa-fred-xavier-trust|Fred on Xavier — "He trusts us. We earned that trust."]]

### Young People's Journeys (evidence the alternative works)

Outcome stories that show what happens when young people are diverted into community-led programs instead of detention.

- [[stories/cb-cultural-leadership|CB: Cultural Responsibility and Leadership]]
- [[stories/ms-future-entrepreneur|MS: Disconnected Youth to Tourism Entrepreneur]]

pages.title: June's Patch
pages.excerpt: A network of therapeutic gardens providing nature prescriptions for Queensland healthcare workers — responding to a mental health crisis in the caring professions through land, community, and evidence-based social prescribing.
pages.content:
> A network of therapeutic gardens providing nature prescriptions for Queensland healthcare workers — responding to a mental health crisis in the caring professions through land, community, and evidence-based social prescribing.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-JP | **Tier:** Satellite

## Overview

June's Patch addresses a hidden crisis: the mental health of the people who care for everyone else. Healthcare workers — nurses, doctors, paramedics, allied health staff — face some of the highest rates of burnout, compassion fatigue, and psychological injury of any workforce. June's Patch responds not with clinical programs or EAP services but with something more fundamental: soil, plants, community, and time.

The project creates a network of therapeutic gardens in Queensland, specifically designed as accessible nature prescription sites for healthcare workers. Each garden is a place of refuge, restoration, and reconnection — with nature, with peers, and with a sense of purpose beyond the clinical environment.

The name honours the tradition of kitchen and patch gardens as places of care and nourishment — practical, grounded, and rooted in relationship.

## The Problem

Healthcare worker burnout and mental health crisis is not new, but its scale has intensified. Structural understaffing, pandemic aftermath, moral injury from systemic failures, and the emotional labour of holding space for suffering day after day — these compound into chronic psychological stress that conventional EAP or clinical responses struggle to address.

Isolation is a particular driver. Healthcare workers often feel they cannot show vulnerability to colleagues or employers. June's Patch creates spaces where showing up, getting hands dirty, and being in community is the intervention — no disclosure required.

## Model

### Therapeutic Gardens
Nature-based environments designed according to evidence from therapeutic landscape research — sensory richness, productive growing, safe enclosure, and community scale.

### Nature Prescriptions for Healthcare Workers
Partnerships with healthcare organisations enable formal referral pathways — a GP or manager can write a "nature prescription" directing a worker to June's Patch, normalising help-seeking and embedding the program within existing health infrastructure.

### Evidence-Based Research
The project builds an evidence base for therapeutic horticulture as a mental health intervention for healthcare workers — contributing to the growing literature on social prescribing and informing future program design.

### Phased Community Ownership
In line with ACT's [[designing-for-obsolescence|Designing for Obsolescence]] philosophy, June's Patch is structured for phased community ownership of individual garden sites. Healthcare worker communities become stewards of their own spaces, reducing dependence on ACT and deepening the ownership that makes therapeutic environments work.

## LCAA Phase

**Listen + Action** — The project begins with deep listening to the experience of healthcare workers: what is actually happening, what does care look and feel like, what do people need beyond what the clinical system can offer? That listening shapes action: building the gardens, establishing the prescribing pathways, growing the community of stewards.

pages.title: June's Patch Healthcare Retreat
pages.excerpt: We run healthcare-worker retreats at Black Cockatoo Valley as an extension of the June's Patch practice — nature prescription at residential scale, grounded in soil, quiet, and shared meals. No disclosure required. The work is the rest.
pages.content:
> We run healthcare-worker retreats at Black Cockatoo Valley as an extension of the [[junes-patch|June's Patch]] practice — nature prescription at residential scale, grounded in soil, quiet, and shared meals. No disclosure required. The work is the rest.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-FM-EXP-junes-patch-healthcare-retreat | **Cluster:** [[act-farm|ACT Farm]]

## What it is

June's Patch is ACT's network of therapeutic gardens for healthcare workers — nature prescription, evidence-backed, phased to community ownership. The retreat offer at BCV extends that practice from day-visit gardens to residential time on Country.

Healthcare workers come here for 2–5 nights. We hold the space quietly. There's no therapy program, no group work we expect people to opt into, no disclosure required. People garden if they want to garden. They walk. They eat. They sleep. That is the intervention.

## Who it's for

- Nurses, doctors, paramedics, allied health workers, midwives, aged-care staff
- Teams from healthcare organisations running peer restoration programs
- Clinicians carrying moral injury, burnout, or compassion fatigue who need somewhere that isn't a clinical environment
- Cohorts referred via partner health services using nature-prescription pathways

We're not running a medical intervention. Anyone who needs acute mental health care needs that, not this.

## What happens

- Arrival late afternoon, a light meal, an early night
- Mornings are slow — garden time, a walk, breakfast whenever it happens
- Afternoons might include optional practice sessions (horticulture, food preserving, quiet making) or might not
- Shared evening meals using produce from here and from [[the-harvest|The Harvest]]
- Optional peer circles — opt in, not opt out
- Departure with no homework

The design principle: do less than a traditional retreat. The land does the work if we get out of its way.

## Price, duration, capacity

| Item | Detail |
|------|--------|
| **Duration** | 2–5 nights |
| **Capacity** | 4–12 per retreat |
| **Price** | Tiered — partner-health subsidy (priority for healthcare workers referred via partner organisations), individual self-funded, employer-funded |
| **Includes** | Accommodation, meals, garden and land access, light hosting |
| **Optional** | Peer circles, horticulture sessions, [[the-harvest|Harvest]] day |
| **Season** | Year-round, subject to land capacity |

## Ecosystem links

- [[junes-patch|June's Patch]] — the project this retreat extends
- [[act-farm|ACT Farm]] — studio practice and hosting
- [[black-cockatoo-valley|Black Cockatoo Valley]] — the land
- [[the-harvest|The Harvest]] — food layer and Witta workshop pairings
- [[caring-for-those-who-care|Caring for Those Who Care]] — the wider frame

## Related case studies

- [[case-studies/junes-patch-year-one-2025|June's Patch Year One — the JCF partnership, 2024–2025]] — first year of the multi-year June Canavan Foundation partnership. Evidence that healthcare-worker wellbeing responds to nature + community + purpose, and the justification for the Year Two Planting Projects pivot.

## How to inquire

Referral and self-inquiry both welcome. Tell us whether you're referring via a healthcare partner or coming individually, and the rough window you're looking at. Inquiries go through `/experiences/junes-patch-healthcare-retreat` on the ACT Farm site.

## LCAA Phase

In the [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]], the [[junes-patch|June's Patch]] Healthcare Retreat is the Listen phase made residential — nature prescription extended from day-visit gardens to 2–5 nights on Country. The design principle is *do less than a traditional retreat; the land does the work if we get out of its way*. Here's how the four phases show up:

- **Listen** — early arrival, light meal, an early night; the slowness itself as the intervention
- **Curiosity** — opt-in (not opt-out) peer circles, optional practice sessions; the inquiry the participant chooses, when they're ready
- **Action** — garden time, walks, food preserving, quiet making; a shared evening meal using produce from BCV and [[the-harvest|The Harvest]]
- **Art** — departure with no homework; the durable register of having been somewhere that wasn't a clinical environment

Not a medical intervention. The work is the rest.

pages.title: June's Patch Year One — the JCF partnership, 2024–2025
pages.excerpt: A multi-year partnership between A Curious Tractor and the June Canavan Foundation, named for Dr June Canavan's belief in the health–nature intersection. Year One was supposed to be about nature prescriptions for healthcare workers. What it actually became was a community that runs as much online as on the land, and that is now pivoting into food production as the next form of therapy.
pages.content:
> A multi-year partnership between A Curious Tractor and the June Canavan Foundation, named for Dr June Canavan's belief in the health–nature intersection. Year One was supposed to be about nature prescriptions for healthcare workers. What it actually became was a community that runs as much online as on the land, and that is now pivoting into food production as the next form of therapy.

**Status:** Published | **Code:** ACT-FM-CS-junes-patch-year-one-2025 | **Cluster:** [[act-farm|ACT Farm]]

## Snapshot

| Item | Detail |
|------|--------|
| **When** | Year One reporting period: October 2024 – September 2025 (Annual Report to JCF, September 2025) |
| **Partnership** | 3-year commitment between ACT and the [[june-canavan-foundation|June Canavan Foundation]] |
| **Site** | [[black-cockatoo-valley|Black Cockatoo Valley]] (pilot), Witta community; Sunshine Coast region |
| **Who it serves** | Queensland healthcare workers — doctors, nurses, allied health — carrying post-COVID burnout, isolation, trauma |
| **Network** | [[june-canavan-foundation|June Canavan Foundation]] · Sunshine Coast Hospital Foundation · University of the Sunshine Coast (research) · Bond University (adjacent leader-wellbeing study) · local farms and producers · BCV / Witta community |
| **Related experience** | [[experiences/junes-patch-healthcare-retreat|June's Patch Healthcare Retreat]] |
| **Year Two pivot** | June's Patch Planting Projects — market garden supplying schools, community centres, healthcare facilities, food relief |

## What happened

[[junes-patch|June's Patch]] was designed as a "nature prescription" program for healthcare workers: therapeutic gardens, time on Country, meals from the land, no disclosure required. The first year of the JCF partnership kept that mission and stretched its shape.

Year One's design centred on residential and garden-based gatherings at [[black-cockatoo-valley|BCV]]. What we learned in the first twelve months: healthcare workers' schedules don't bend to a weekend-retreat calendar — nights, shifts, leave blocks, exhaustion. If the program only exists in person, most of the people it's for can't reach it. So we expanded.

Online community groups became 24/7 support networks that sat alongside physical gatherings. Hybrid engagement — in-person at BCV, digital between — turned out to be the format the cohort actually needed. Friendships and peer support structures formed that have outlasted the program window.

Meanwhile, the pilot site at BCV was established, partnerships strengthened with the Sunshine Coast Hospital Foundation and University of the Sunshine Coast, and ACT started treating healthcare-worker wellbeing as a long-horizon problem the partnership is equipped for: not a retreat product, a practice.

## What we did

- **We kept the mission but loosened the format.** The "no disclosure required, the work is the rest" promise stayed. The insistence that this had to be a residential weekend softened — a healthcare worker with nothing left at the end of a shift needs somewhere to go *that night*, not a retreat ticket in three months.
- **We built the online layer.** Dedicated community groups gave healthcare workers a 24/7 peer channel in a cohort that actually understood the rhythm of their work. This wasn't a Facebook group we threw up; it was facilitated with the same care as a residential session.
- **We ran physical gatherings at BCV** as the anchor. The pilot site was established; trips and cohort visits are running quarterly across the Sunshine Coast region.
- **We partnered with researchers.** The University of the Sunshine Coast is measuring wellbeing outcomes across the program. Bond University sits alongside through the adjacent Supporting NFP Leaders and Social Entrepreneurs study. This is not "we did a survey" evidence — it's properly designed research, on a timeline.
- **We strengthened the institutional ring.** Sunshine Coast Hospital Foundation deepened as a sector partner. Potential auspicing conversations advanced. Local farms, producers, and the Witta community moved from supportive bystanders to integrated parts of the program.
- **We documented the evolution.** The Annual Report to JCF is transparent about where the year went — not a stock "on-track" narrative, a real account of how the program changed shape and why. JCF's trust-based, multi-year philanthropy is what made that honesty possible.

## What the work produced

**A hybrid operating model for healthcare-worker wellbeing.** June's Patch now runs as online community + periodic physical gatherings + research partnership, rather than as a residential-retreat program. That model scales where the residential-only version couldn't.

**A cohort that stays.** Healthcare workers who came through the program have formed lasting friendships and peer-support structures that don't depend on the program to continue. That's the difference between a retreat and a network.

**A testimony that captures what the work feels like.** One Registered Nurse from the Sunshine Coast:

> "June's Patch gave me a space to breathe and reconnect with why I became a nurse. The garden became my sanctuary between shifts."

**An Annual Report that tells the truth.** JCF's trust-based funding let us report what actually happened rather than what the original proposal said would happen. That honesty is rare in philanthropy and it's what makes the Year Two pivot credible.

**A research baseline.** Year One lays down the evidence base — wellbeing measures, participation data, partnership structures — that Year Two and Three can demonstrate real movement against.

## The Year Two pivot: June's Patch Planting Projects

Year One proved that healthcare worker wellbeing responds to nature, food, and community. Year Two takes that finding and extends it into community food security.

**June's Patch Planting Projects** is the market-garden evolution. Healthcare workers who garden therapeutically also grow produce for local schools, community centres, healthcare facilities, and food-relief partners. The same plant that supports a nurse's wellbeing feeds a classroom.

Rationale:

- Healthcare workers have told us they want *purpose beyond clinical roles* — the market garden gives them that without asking them to do more care work
- Sunshine Coast food insecurity is a live problem — producing for local schools and food relief partners matters here
- The program becomes more durable when it produces something beyond its own cohort — schools, families, and food-relief partners become stakeholders in June's Patch continuing

Immediate priorities (Year Two):

- Garden infrastructure — raised beds, irrigation, storage
- Partnership formalisation with local schools and community centres for produce distribution
- Volunteer recruitment across healthcare workers, community members, families
- Educational programs connecting gardening, nutrition, and wellness

## What we learned

- **Format flexibility outperforms format purity.** A residential-only program would have reached fewer healthcare workers and reached them shallower. Hybrid is not a compromise; it is the right shape for this cohort.
- **Trust-based multi-year philanthropy lets programs evolve.** Year One shifted meaningfully from the original design. A single-year, output-locked grant would have forced us to either fake delivery or break the relationship. JCF's multi-year commitment made the honest pivot possible.
- **"Therapy" shows up as purpose, not just rest.** Healthcare workers told us repeatedly that contributing to something beyond their clinical work — a garden, a community, a meal — was as therapeutic as the quiet. Year Two is built on that finding.
- **Research partnerships are program partners, not reporting overhead.** The University of the Sunshine Coast work isn't happening so we can show charts — it's shaping the design.
- **The BCV pilot is necessary but not sufficient.** One site proves the pattern. Fifteen sites (the stated scope) will test whether the pattern travels. Year Two is the scale-out.

## Evidence

- **June's Patch Annual Report — FY26 JCF Partnership** (September 2025, reporting Oct 2024 – Sep 2025) — the primary source for this case study
- Testimony: "The garden became my sanctuary between shifts" — Registered Nurse, Sunshine Coast (quoted in Annual Report)
- University of the Sunshine Coast research partnership — in progress, wellbeing outcome measures
- Sunshine Coast Hospital Foundation partnership correspondence
- BCV pilot site — live, photographable, visitable; part of the [[black-cockatoo-valley|BCV]] operating footprint
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — planned story capture for healthcare-worker narratives with consent

pages.title: Justice & Community Funding Landscape
pages.excerpt: Where the money actually flows — and where it doesn't. Australian government, procurement, and philanthropic spend across community services, youth justice, and adjacent sectors.
pages.content:
> Where the money actually flows — and where it doesn't. Australian government, procurement, and philanthropic spend across community services, youth justice, and adjacent sectors.

## Overview

JusticeHub maintains a unified view of public spending, philanthropy, and procurement across Australia. The data is messy — sourced from ROGS national reporting, AusTender contracts, philanthropic disclosures, state grant registers — but the pattern is clear: **government spend dwarfs philanthropy by two orders of magnitude**, and most of it concentrates in a handful of states and intermediaries.

## Top Sectors by Total Dollars

| State | Sector | Records | Orgs | Total | ALMA-Linked |
|-------|--------|---------|------|-------|-------------|
| QLD | community_services | 86,399 | 35,256 | **$31.8B** | 78,852 |
| QLD | national_reporting | 103 | 5 | $17.8B | 0 |
| VIC | national_reporting | 103 | 5 | $15.5B | 63 |
| NSW | national_reporting | 103 | 5 | $14.5B | 0 |
| WA | national_reporting | 103 | 5 | $6.6B | 63 |
| NT | national_reporting | 103 | 5 | $5.0B | 0 |
| **QLD** | **youth_justice** | **10,926** | **7,004** | **$4.1B** | **10,897** |
| QLD | legal_services | 32,635 | 20,740 | $3.0B | 32,568 |
| NSW | child_protection | 1,597 | 1,193 | $2.7B | 1,340 |
| NSW | community_services | 5,577 | 4,405 | $2.1B | 3,145 |
| (national) | **philanthropic** | 654 | 413 | **$1.45B** | 494 |
| NSW | procurement | 1,885 | 1,085 | $1.4B | 1,865 |
| WA | philanthropic | 160 | 77 | $952M | 129 |
| QLD | education | 3,237 | 1,539 | $675M | 3,071 |
| ACT | procurement | 1,190 | 706 | $566M | 1,131 |

## The Three Things This Reveals

### 1. Philanthropy is a rounding error

National philanthropic disclosure totals **$1.45B across 413 organisations**. QLD community services alone is **$31.8B**. Philanthropic giving — the part of the system most visible in the press, most romanticised in donor circles, and most over-represented in funder relationships — is barely 5% of one state's community services budget.

This is why the [[funding-transparency|funding transparency]] argument matters. The dollars that actually shape outcomes are the procurement and grants the public never sees clearly.

### 2. QLD is the proof-of-concept jurisdiction

ALMA-linkage rate (interventions matched to funding records) is **above 90% in QLD** across community services, youth justice, legal services, and procurement. It's near zero in most other states and absent from the national ROGS rollups. JusticeHub's evidence base is presently a QLD model — for good reason, since the data was richest there — but the scaling story for 2026–2027 is replicating the linkage in NSW, VIC, and WA.

### 3. The numbers don't follow the evidence

QLD youth justice spend: **$4.1B across 7,004 organisations**. The [[alma-intervention-portfolio|top-scoring interventions in ALMA's portfolio]] — DIYDG, Rumbalara, Oochiumpa, Mulungu — are typically funded between $50K and $5M each. The dollars concentrate at the top end (large NGOs, Legal Aid, departmental programs); the evidence concentrates at the bottom (small ACCOs).

This is the gap [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] exists to make visible.

## Caveats

- **National reporting rows** (103 records per state) are aggregate ROGS lines, not granular spending. They appear large because they're rolled-up totals.
- **"Procurement" sectors** capture government contracts visible in AusTender — they miss state-level procurement that doesn't publish.
- **ALMA linkage is a quality signal**: where it's high, the data has been triangulated against intervention records; where it's zero, the dollars are visible but not yet matched to outcomes.

pages.title: JusticeHub
pages.excerpt: Evidence-based justice alternatives — proving what works, routing capital to what heals.
pages.content:
> Evidence-based justice alternatives — proving what works, routing capital to what heals.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-JH | **Tier:** Ecosystem

> 📣 **Narrative claims store:** [`wiki/narrative/justicehub/`](../narrative/justicehub/INDEX.md) — every public argument we have made about JusticeHub, STAY, The Three Circles, Staying, and The Brave Ones. The whole constellation in one place. Read this before drafting any new pitch or post. Run `node scripts/narrative-draft.mjs justicehub --funder minderoo --channel pitch --length long` to assemble a draft brief from the under-deployed claims.
>
> **Constellation files (sources):**
> - [[the-full-idea|The Full Idea]] — STAY's complete walkthrough (3-year program, 7 method books, 10 communities, the library)
> - [[three-circles|The Three Circles]] — canonical Minderoo pitch ($2.9M / Lucy Stronach)
> - [[staying|Staying — Country & Council]] — methodology layer of the Three Circles
> - [[the-brave-ones|The Brave Ones]] — photographic art companion (counter-mugshot)
> - This file — the platform layer

## What It Is

JusticeHub is ACT's evidence platform for justice alternatives. It catalogs community-led programs, tracks their outcomes, and provides the fiduciary evidence needed to divert funds from detention to healing.

It is the **evidence layer** of [[third-reality|The Third Reality]].

## Cluster Context

JusticeHub should be read as a constellation, not a lone product page. The durable cluster logic lives in [[projects/justicehub/README|JusticeHub Cluster]], while the live proof layer should come through [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] and the public sites. That is how the platform, pitch, methodology, and art companion stay aligned instead of drifting into separate truths.

## Key People

JusticeHub should keep a curated people layer, not a full stakeholder mirror. The load-bearing figures are the ones who explain how the field holds together across system design, lived experience, and community authority.

- [[benjamin-knight|Benjamin Knight]] — ACT co-founder and the main systems builder connecting JusticeHub to the wider ACT stack
- [[brodie-germaine|Brodie Germaine]] — lived-experience justice practitioner whose work makes the alternatives legible on the ground
- [[kristy-bloomfield|Kristy Bloomfield]] — Oonchiumpa cultural authority and one of the clearest community anchors in the JusticeHub proof layer
- [[vic|Vic]] — public transformation-to-service narrative that helps the evidence read as human truth, not only platform logic

The broader storyteller, partner, and mentor network should remain primarily in [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] and in the source-bridge layer unless a person becomes structurally necessary across multiple canonical pages.

## Scale (April 2026)

- **1,000+** verified alternative models mapped
- **430** models with evidence data
- **$94.6B** in funding tracked
- **98,418** organizations mapped
- **85%** recidivism rate for youth detention
- Indigenous young people face **24x** higher incarceration rates

## The Economic Case

| Approach | Annual Cost per Child | Success Rate |
|----------|--------------------|-------------|
| Youth detention | $1.3M/year ($3,634.90/day national average) | 15% (85% recidivism) |
| Community-led alternatives | ~$14,000 | 97x cheaper |

This isn't just better for communities — it's better economics. Community models are 97x cheaper than detention, and every dollar diverted creates compounding savings.

## Three Pathways

| Audience | Entry Point | Tool |
|---------|-------------|------|
| Youth | "I need help" | Youth Scout |
| Organizations | ALMA Network | Directory + evidence tools |
| Policymakers | Evidence dashboards | Cost Calculator, System Map, Impact Dashboard |

## Key Features

- **ALMA AI Chat** — conversational interface to the evidence base
- **Cost Calculator** — real-time cost comparison of detention vs community alternatives
- **System Map** — visual mapping of the justice ecosystem
- **Impact Dashboard** — outcome data across programs
- **Learning Trips** — international study visits (e.g. Spain [[diagrama|Diagrama]] model)

## Funding Need

JusticeHub needs **$500K** to scale nationally.

## ALMA (Australian Living Map of Alternatives)

The "what works" layer sitting on top of funding data:
- Evidence-based interventions mapped by topic and geography
- 9 topic domains: child-protection, community-led, diversion, family-services, indigenous, legal-services, ndis, prevention, youth-justice
- Cross-referenced with CivicGraph entity graph (56% linkage rate)

## Local Proof Points

### BG Fit ([[mount-isa|Mount Isa]])
- Reduced youth police contact from average of 5 incidents to less than 1
- Community-led physical activity and mentoring program
- The wider Mount Isa proof layer also includes [[campfire|CAMPFIRE]], founded by [[brodie-germaine|Brodie Germaine]], where cultural immersion, on-Country camps, and mentorship become a justice alternative rather than an afterthought

### [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] (Alice Springs)
- 95% reduction in anti-social behavior
- Place-based Indigenous-led program

### Confit Pathways (Sydney)
- 60% reduction in recidivism
- Diversionary program with wraparound support

## Capital Routing Vision

### Impact-Weighted Quadratic Funding (ImpactQF)
- Integrating Gitcoin's open-source Allo Protocol for programmable capital allocation
- Matching funds distributed based on verified community outcomes, not popularity
- ALMA AI scores projects → capital follows evidence

### Hypercerts
- Semi-fungible tokens recording verified social outcomes
- Persistent, interoperable digital records of impactful work
- Any funder or government treasury can audit

### Catalytic Capital Framing
Following [[global-precedents|East African precedents]], JusticeHub funding is positioned as "catalytic capital" — high-leverage investment unlocking massive downstream savings.

## Connection to CivicGraph

JusticeHub evidence sits within the broader CivicGraph data model:
- [[grantscope|GrantScope (CivicGraph)]] is the underlying technical substrate that makes the JusticeHub evidence and query layer operational rather than aspirational
- `justice_funding` table: 145,242 records (86% linked to entities)
- `alma_interventions`: 1,357 records (56% linked)
- `crime_stats_lga`: 57,435 records
- `outcomes_metrics`: 8,962 records across all states
- `rogs_justice_spending`: 8,873 records

## Identity & Brand

### Purpose
JusticeHub exists to centre lived experience in youth justice reform. The platform connects research, evidence, and service directories to the people who actually know what works — communities, practitioners, and young people themselves. It is not a case management tool. It is infrastructure that communities can own, adapt, and use to advocate for alternatives to detention.

### Philosophy

| Principle | How It Shows Up |
|-----------|----------------|
| **Community authority comes first** | Lived-experience advisors shape platform direction. Community organisations control their data. |
| **Evidence is story, not surveillance** | Research hub indexes evidence without profiling individuals. Stories carry context. |
| **Build for handover** | Open-source platform. Designed for community ownership. |
| **Make with lived experience** | Pathways for lived-experience leadership in justice advocacy. |
| **Identity before product** | We start with who holds authority in justice spaces, then build tools around that. |

### Brand Voice
- Evidence-based but community-led
- "Justice infrastructure" not "justice tech"
- Centre young people's agency, not their trauma
- Never describe young people as "offenders" — they are system-impacted
- Lead with what works, not what's broken

### LCAA in Practice

| Stage | How It Manifests |
|-------|-----------------|
| **Listen** | AI research chat surfaces community voice alongside policy evidence. Service directory built from community knowledge. |
| **Curiosity** | International comparisons ([[diagrama|Diagrama]], Spain). Inquiry database indexes what's been tried. |
| **Action** | [[contained|CONTAINED]] art installation brings justice reform into public consciousness. Service directory connects youth to support. |
| **Art** | CONTAINED exhibitions make system change felt, not abstract. Network visualisations reveal hidden connections. |

### What Makes This Different
Most justice platforms are built for the system. JusticeHub is built for the communities the system impacts. The research hub doesn't just index policy — it foregrounds lived experience evidence. The service directory doesn't just list providers — it maps networks of community support. The [[contained|CONTAINED]] program doesn't just advocate — it makes the case for change through art and direct experience.

## Engagement & Partnership Strategy

### Stakeholder Tiers
JusticeHub reaches 63,112 scored entities across the sector:

| Tier | Score | Count | Approach |
|------|-------|-------|----------|
| Hot leads | 80+ | 16 | Personal outreach only |
| Nurture | 60–79 | 3,760 | Warm broadcast |
| Cold awareness | 40–59 | ~3,700 | Campaign email + social |
| Organic only | <40 | 59,336 | No contact |

### Partnership Asks by Type
- **Funders:** Fund specific tour stops ($25K–$75K each) or JusticeHub platform ($500K total)
- **Allies:** Feature their work in CONTAINED Room 3; amplify through networks
- **Decision-makers:** Walk through CONTAINED; nominate peers; use data in submissions
- **Research partners:** Rohan Lulham (USyd) offered research partnership — *"keen to do some research around the concept"*

### Key Partner Organisations
- **Minderoo Foundation** — funder prospect (Lucy Stronach, score 79, email sent)
- **Uniting** — Emma Maiden (Director Advocacy): wants NSW MPs to walk through
- **Reconciliation WA** — Megan McCormack (CEO): state-level reconciliation leadership
- **EPIC Pathways** (Brisbane) — Rhian Miller: QLD youth services partner
- **Prevention Not Detention Tasmania** — Loic Fery: coalition ready to organise TAS stop
- **Just Reinvest** — Nicole Mekler: advocacy co-partner

### Comms Principles
Direct, evidence-based, community-centred. What not to say:
- "Excited to announce" → say "This is happening"
- "We believe" → say "The evidence shows"
- "At-risk youth" → say "young people affected by the system"
- Every stat has a named source; no rounding up; no "approximately"

## Technical Identity

| Element | Value |
|---------|-------|
| Framework | Next.js 14.2.35, React 18, TypeScript |
| Database | Supabase (3 instances: main, YJSF, QJT) + ChromaDB |
| AI | Claude, OpenAI, Groq |
| Hosting | Vercel |
| Live URL | [justicehub.com.au](https://justicehub.com.au) |
| Alternate | justicehub.act.place |
| GitHub | [act-now-coalition/justicehub-platform](https://github.com/act-now-coalition/justicehub-platform) |
| Local dev | `npm run dev` → http://localhost:3003 |

## Infrastructure & Operations

### Supabase Instances

JusticeHub runs across three Supabase instances by design — separating platform data from partner-specific datasets. Core key tables: `empathy_ledger_core` (story integration), `story_workspaces` (collaborative editing), `services` (support service directory), `organizations` (service providers), `art_innovation` (Contained art programs).

### External Integrations

- **GHL CRM:** Pipeline "Justice", tags: `youth-justice`, `justicehub`, `contained`.
- **Xero:** Tracking category `JH`, project codes `JH-CORE` and `JH-CONTAINED`.
- **Firecrawl:** Automated web scraping for the Queensland service directory.
- **Notion:** Research and content management integration.

### Platform Routes

| Section | URL |
|---------|-----|

## Public Voice

*How JusticeHub describes itself on its public website (justicehub.com.au, captured 2026-04-07)*

### Hero Statement

> Australia locks up children. The alternative exists.

The site leads not with JusticeHub as a platform, but as a data statement: "1,000 community models proving it works better and costs less." The positioning is declarative — "this is the transparency engine for youth justice in Australia" — rather than pitch-style.

### Three Doors (Audience Entry Points)

Named by role, not urgency:
- **"I need help"** — direct to crisis/service support, "No judgment, just options"
- **"I do the work"** — ALMA Network framing, peer-to-peer
- **"I fund or shape policy"** — evidence first, "Make decisions based on data, not lobby groups"

The three-door design is notably non-hierarchical. Young people in need get top billing alongside funders.

### Wall of Proof (Live Data, 2026-04-07)

| Metric | Internal Wiki | Public Site (live) |
|--------|--------------|-------------------|
| Verified models | "1,000+" | **1,387** |
| Evidence-backed | "430 with evidence data" | 57 proven/effective, 474 promising |
| Avg cost/YP | "$14,000" | **$15K** |
| Recidivism (detention) | 85% | 84% |
| Cost comparison | 97x cheaper | **86x** cheaper (updated) |

The public site shows updated figures. Internal wiki cost/recidivism data is from an earlier state — worth syncing.

On Indigenous-led models, the site says: *"These models don't need Western evidence frameworks to prove they work — they have 65,000 years of proof."*

### CONTAINED Tour Framing

> "One shipping container. Three rooms. Thirty minutes. Touring Australia. We are building it as we go because the people who need to see it cannot wait for perfect."

Tour dates (2026): Mount Druitt (May), Brisbane (May), Adelaide (June), Townsville (July), Perth (August), Tennant Creek (September — **confirmed**). Each stop costs $30K to stage. SA has the starkest ratio in the country: $50M detention vs $8M community.

### Number Divergence: Platform Name vs Mission

The site's SEO title is "JusticeHub — Empowering Youth Through Storytelling" but the live experience is evidence-based reform infrastructure at scale. The SEO title undersells the platform for any funder who googles before a meeting.

## LCAA Phase

In the [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]], JusticeHub is the **evidence layer** of [[third-reality|The Third Reality]] — the **Curiosity** infrastructure that catalogs what works, surfaces it for funders and policymakers, and connects young people, communities, and decision-makers to community-led alternatives to detention.

LCAA arc for JusticeHub:
- **Listen** — three doors named by role rather than urgency (*"I need help"*, *"I do the work"*, *"I fund or shape policy"*); ALMA AI chat surfacing community voice alongside policy evidence; service directory built from community knowledge
- **Curiosity** — 1,387 verified models, 430 with evidence data, 98K orgs mapped, $94.6B funding tracked; international comparisons ([[diagrama|Diagrama]], Spain); the cost case (community-led ~$15K/year vs detention ~$1.3M/year, 86x cheaper)
- **Action** — Cost Calculator, System Map, Impact Dashboard, Learning Trips; capital routing via Allo Protocol and Hypercerts; service directory connecting youth to support; on-the-ground proof from BG Fit, [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]], and [[confit-pathways|ConFit Pathways]]
- **Art** — [[contained|CONTAINED]] — the touring shipping container exhibition that brings justice reform into public consciousness and makes system change felt, not abstract; portraits from [[the-brave-ones|The Brave Ones]] live on its inside walls

The platform is built for the communities the system impacts, not for the system itself.

## System Position

JusticeHub is one of ACT's flagship public fields, but it is not supposed to carry the whole system alone:

- the wiki holds the durable platform framing, reform logic, cluster structure, and argument spine
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] should carry the live story, portrait, and documentation layer
- the JusticeHub website should stay the spoke surface for evidence, proof, and entry points without becoming the only place where the truth lives

This is why JusticeHub needs to stay attached to [[living-website-operating-system|Living Website Operating System]] and to the Studio's wider economic and cultural logic in [[art/business/studio-business-model|Studio Business Model]]. CONTAINED, the proof wall, and the reform surface are all part of one field.
