pages.title: Spinifex Residential — Getting Through to the Hard Cases
pages.excerpt: Spinifex Res Youth
pages.content:
> Spinifex Res Youth

> When we first started going in there, the staff were sceptical. After about the fourth session, the kids started waiting for us at the gate.

## Summary

BG Fit's program at Spinifex Residential works with young people in out-of-home care and the justice system, using sport to build trust.

## Story

Spinifex Residential in Mount Isa is where some of our toughest kids end up. These are young people who've been removed from home, who've been through the justice system, some of them multiple times. They're angry, they're hurt, and most of them don't trust adults.

When we first started going in there, the staff were sceptical. They'd seen programs come and go. The kids would test us — not listening, walking off, trying to get a rise. But we kept coming back.

After about the fourth session, something changed. The kids started waiting for us at the gate. They'd have their shoes on, ready to go. One boy who wouldn't even look at us in week one was leading the warm-up by week six.

The residential staff told us the kids are calmer on the days we come. There's less incidents. They sleep better. It's like they need somewhere to put all that energy and emotion, and the gym gives them that.

We don't lecture them. We don't ask about their charges or their history. We just train with them. We treat them like young athletes, not like problems. I think that's what makes the difference.

One of the boys there, he wants to get into boxing. We're trying to connect him with a boxing gym for when he gets out. That's the pathway — not just keeping them busy while they're inside, but connecting them to something on the outside.

## Backlinks

- [[bg-fit|BG Fit]]

pages.title: Staying — Country & Council
pages.excerpt: The flagship reflection for STAY lives at The Kettle. Read that first if you want the why in Ben's voice — the room at Oonchiumpa, Diagrama, and the four-layer infrastructure that makes the kettle legible.
pages.content:
> **The flagship reflection for STAY lives at [[../../synthesis/the-kettle|The Kettle]].** Read that first if you want the *why* in Ben's voice — the room at Oonchiumpa, Diagrama, and the four-layer infrastructure that makes the kettle legible.

> ⚠️ **2026-04-08 framing change.** This page was originally drafted as a standalone Minderoo pitch. After review of the canonical Three Circles proposal (`wiki/raw/2026-04-07-jh-three-circles-proposal.md`) — which Lucy Stronach is already warm on at $2.9M / 3 years with 10 anchor communities — **Staying has been reframed as the *methodology layer* inside Three Circles, not a competing pitch.**
>
> The canonical pitch lives at **[[three-circles|The Three Circles]]**.
> Staying is the name of the *practice* the Circle Two embedded storytelling team does, plus the per-young-person *Journal* artefact added to *The Country We're Building*.
>
> Everything below is preserved as the alternative-shape working draft. Numbers, communities, tiers, European-only framing — all superseded by Three Circles. **Do not pitch this version.** Refer to `[[three-circles]]` for the canonical proposal.

> *A three-year accompaniment of community-led youth justice in seven places.*

**Status:** ⚠️ Superseded by [[three-circles|Three Circles]] as a pitch — preserved here as the methodology + alternative-shape working draft | **Cluster:** Methodology + creative artefact (now lives inside Circle Two) | **Original envelope (no longer the ask):** Foundation $1.8M · Recommended $3.43M · Full ambition $6M (over 3 years)

## What it is

A 3-year program in which a small team rotates through 7 Australian communities — one in each state — accompanying community-led youth justice work, photographing it, journaling it, and producing a bound book per young person at the end. In Year 2, every community sends a young person and a support person on a focused exchange visit to **one** European country — [[diagrama|Diagrama]] in Spain, Halt in Holland, or the Children's Hearings system in Scotland — and brings the experience back. After 3 years it culminates in seven community-led launches and a published book — the largest collection of community-led youth justice evidence ever assembled in this country.

The word **Staying** is the methodology. Every other youth justice program leaves. Staying is the move.

The subtitle **Country & Council** is non-negotiable. *Country* is the place and the people on it. *Council* is the form of community-led decision-making. Both structures are the spine of the program.

## Cluster Context

Staying should remain a methodology page inside the [[projects/justicehub/README|JusticeHub Cluster]], not drift into a competing standalone pitch. The wiki holds the method and its relationship to [[three-circles|The Three Circles]] and [[justicehub|JusticeHub]], [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] should hold the living proof through journals, portraits, and stories, and the websites should compose those layers through the [[../../technical/wiki-project-and-work-sync-contract|Wiki Project and Work Sync Contract]] and [[../../concepts/living-website-operating-system|Living Website Operating System]].

## Why this exists

Australia spends $3.9M to detain a single child for 3 years. For roughly the cost of detaining 1.5 children, Staying runs for 3 years across 7 communities, reaches ~50 young people, takes Aboriginal Elders and tribal council members to Spain, and produces the largest evidence base of community-led youth justice ever assembled in this country.

The pattern Staying makes legible is older than fintech — Tyson Yunkaporta's *Sand Talk*, Elinor Ostrom's commons work, [[diagrama|Diagrama]]'s three decades in Murcia. [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] is the *world model* that holds it. [[the-brave-ones|The Brave Ones]] is its human face. [[contained|CONTAINED]] is the room you walk into. **Staying is the program that produces all of it.**

It is also the answer to the only question philanthropic capital ever actually asks: *does it work, and how do we know?* Staying answers by staying long enough to be in the proof.

See the synthesis: [[the-edge-is-where-the-healing-is-justicehub-as-the-world-model-for-community-led|The Edge Is Where the Healing Is]].

## Three movements

| Year | Name | Where | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Year 1** | *Listen* | 7 Australian communities | 4 months on (rotating visits) + 8 months virtual support |
| **Year 2** | *Compare* | Distributed European exchange — each community sends **2 people** (1 young person + 1 support) to **one** of [[diagrama|Diagrama]] (Spain), Halt (Holland), or Children's Hearings (Scotland) — focused short visit, full capture, return home | 4 months on in AU + the European exchange visits + reciprocal European visits to AU |
| **Year 3** | *Tell* | Back to the 7 communities + 7 community-led launches | 4 months on + 8 months journal production & launches |

Three acts. Funders, audiences, books all need three acts. Listen / Compare / Tell.

## Team

**1 FTE lead + 1 support person — two people.** Lean on purpose. Doesn't overwhelm a community when it arrives, and fits inside a $1M/year ceiling.

## Cadence

- **4 months on** — heavy engagement, rotating visits per community, in person, longer per-visit stays so each trip earns its travel cost
- **8 months off** — back home in Brisbane, processing, photographing, building journals, prepping next round, doing the European exchange logistics in Year 2
- **One community close to Brisbane** for cheap, frequent low-friction visits and a shorter feedback loop

## The journal — the centre artefact

> *If the program produces nothing else, the journals are the proof.*

- **Bound book per young person** — A5, hand-stitched, ~80–120 pages
- **One delivery, in Year 3** — the complete bound volume, accumulating quietly across all three years and only printed once everything is in. (Earlier versions of the design had three chapter deliveries; cut to fit the envelope without losing the artefact itself.)
- **Contents:** B&W portraits in [[the-brave-ones|Brave Ones]] discipline, the young person's own handwriting, voice transcripts from [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]], letters from Aunties and uncles, ledger entries of who showed up and when, drawings, marks, place — and the European exchange visit captured as its own chapter
- **Owned by the young person.** Not ACT. Not Minderoo. OCAP/CARE protocols at the data layer through Empathy Ledger. Right of withdrawal at any point.
- **One archival copy** (with explicit consent only) held by ACT for the program's evidence base.

Visual register: the **ledger page**, not the diagram. References — Christian Boltanski, Sophie Calle, Edmund Clark, Theaster Gates, Anselm Kiefer, Judy Watson, Daniel Boyd, Vernon Ah Kee, Tony Albert, Brook Andrew. Hand-made, lived-in, accumulated over time, system-as-marginalia, the young person at the centre. See `tools/three-ripples-ledger.html`.

## Year 3 launches (communities first)

**Seven launches in seven places.** The work goes home. Each of the seven communities hosts a launch on their own terms, in their own venues, with their own people standing in front of their own portraits and journals.

Accompanied by a **published book** — one printed volume that gathers the seven journals (with consent) into a single national artefact. Every electorate office gets a copy.

**National gallery tour deferred to a Year-4 stretch goal.** The institutional tour (NGA / MCA / NGV / regional) is the natural next chapter once Year 3 has landed and proven the work — but it sits outside this $3M envelope and would be raised separately, ideally with the young people and community representatives travelling with the work into the city institutions in Year 4.

## Year 2 — the European exchange

Year 2 is **distributed, not centralised.** No team-in-residence. No one community sends people to all three countries. Each community chooses one European destination that fits the work they're already doing, sends a focused pair, and brings the experience back into the journal and the home community.

**The shape:**

- **2 travellers per community: 1 young person + 1 support person** (Elder, family member, tribal council member, or program lead — chosen by the community, not by ACT)
- **One country per community**, not all three. Each pair goes deep into one place rather than skating across three.
- **Three host geographies**, chosen because they hold practice the rest of the world treats as impossible:
  - **Spain — [[diagrama|Diagrama]]** (Murcia and beyond). The thirty-year proof that community-based youth justice scales. Cornerstone partner; door is already open via the Olga meeting.
  - **Holland — Halt.** Restorative justice infrastructure and the diversion-first prevention model.
  - **Scotland — Children's Hearings system + Whole System Approach.** The political courage to legislate a minimum age of criminal responsibility worth importing.
- **Focused short visits** — long enough to sit inside the practice, short enough to honour the lives travellers leave at home and to keep the budget honest
- **Reciprocal European visits to Australia** — small delegations from each host (Diagrama, Halt, Scottish) travelling to a subset of the seven communities, walking Country with the people they only ever read about
- **Captured in full** — every visit documented end-to-end (photographs, voice, journal entries), and every traveller's experience becomes a chapter in their community's contribution to the Year 3 book

Why this still works as the masterstroke at a fraction of the original budget:

1. Puts a young person and a community Elder on a plane to Europe and into a Spanish, Dutch, or Scottish youth centre. **Those conversations have never happened in this country's history** — and they happen in seven communities at once because every community sends a pair.
2. Inspires the local communities to believe they are *already* doing world-class work — and to see themselves as international peers, not service recipients.
3. Brings Europe to Australia in the same year. The reciprocal visits collapse the centre/periphery framing every philanthropic conversation about Indigenous justice gets stuck in.
4. Turns [[diagrama|Diagrama]], Halt, and the Children's Hearings network from abstract precedents into living relationships, distributed across seven communities.
5. Gives the program its three-act arc — *Listen / Compare / Tell.*
6. Makes Minderoo's gift internationally legible — *"The Minderoo Australian Justice Cohort sent fourteen people to Europe and brought Europe back."*

## Three scales — same program, three sizes

Staying flexes. The architecture is the same at every scale; what moves is *how many communities*, *how big the team*, *how deep Europe goes*, and *what Year 3 produces*. Three honest tiers, so the conversation with a funder is about fit, not negotiation:

| | **Foundation** | **Recommended** | **Full ambition** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Annual flow** | ~$600K/year | ~$1.0M / $1.24M / $1.20M | ~$2.0M/year |
| **3-year total** | **~$1.8M** | **~$3.43M** | **~$6.0M** |
| **Communities** | 5 communities (drop hardest-to-reach 2 states) | 7 communities, one per state | 7 communities + annual national cohort gathering |
| **Team** | 1 FTE lead, no support | 1 FTE lead + 1 support | 2 FTE + 1 support |
| **Cadence** | 3 months on / 9 months virtual | 4 months on / 8 months virtual | 6 months on / 6 months virtual |
| **Year 2 Europe** | Deferred — small Spain scoping trip only (2 ACT staff, no community travellers) | Distributed exchange — 14 travellers (1 young person + 1 support per community), one country each (Spain / Holland / Scotland) | Distributed exchange + reciprocal European visits to AU + one full cohort immersion week per host country |
| **Journal** | Y3 only, simple binding, 1 copy per young person | Y3 only, hand-stitched, 1 copy per young person + 1 archive | **Three chapter deliveries** (Y1/Y2/Y3), hand-stitched, premium binding, multiple copies |
| **Year 3** | 5 community-led launches, no book | 7 community-led launches + 1 published book | 7 community-led launches + book + **national gallery tour** (NGA / MCA / NGV) + every-electorate-office distribution |
| **Cultural review fees** | $50K/year (the floor) | $80K/year | $100K/year + paid Elder council |
| **What it proves** | The methodology works in Australia | The methodology works *and* scales internationally | The methodology becomes a fixture of Australian civic life |
| **Versus detaining 1 child for 3 years** ($3.9M) | 46% of the cost | 88% of the cost | 154% of the cost |

**Recommended is the default pitch.** Foundation is what we go to if Minderoo wants the cap held flat. Full ambition is what we go to if Minderoo (or co-funders) wants the legacy version — and unlocks the national gallery tour without it needing to be raised separately later.

---

## Detailed budget — Recommended tier (~$1M/year, $3.43M total)

This is the **return-pitch shape**. A previous ~$8M / 3-year design was too much; a fuller ~$6.3M version (year-long European team in residence, 2 FTE + 1 support, three journal chapter deliveries, full national gallery tour) was archived to make this fit. Every line below is sized so the program *moves* rather than stalls in funder negotiation. The Foundation and Full ambition tiers above flex this same line structure up and down.

| Line | Year 1 (AU) | Year 2 (AU + Europe exchange) | Year 3 (AU + community launches) | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Core team (1 FTE lead + 1 support) | $220K | $220K | $220K | $660K |
| AU travel + accommodation (4 months on) | $110K | $80K | $110K | $300K |
| Community partnership fees (7 × $50K/yr) | $350K | $350K | $350K | $1.05M |
| European exchange — 14 travellers (1 young person + 1 support per community), one country each | — | $130K | — | $130K |
| European exchange — chaperone team + in-country fixers + capture | — | $50K | — | $50K |
| European reciprocal visits to AU (small Diagrama / Halt / Scottish delegations) | — | $50K | — | $50K |
| Diagrama + Halt + Children's Hearings partnership fees | — | $50K | — | $50K |
| Young person stipends + journal materials (accumulating) | $30K | $40K | $90K | $160K |
| Journal binding + final book production (Y3 only) | — | — | $80K | $80K |
| Equipment, archive, production | $40K | $20K | $20K | $80K |
| Data + tech infra ([[justicehub|JusticeHub]] / ALMA / [[empathy-ledger|EL]] contributions) | $40K | $30K | $30K | $100K |
| Seven community-led launches (Y3) | — | — | $70K | $70K |
| Comms, social, content | $30K | $30K | $40K | $100K |
| Cultural review + Elder governance fees | $80K | $80K | $80K | $240K |
| Operations + admin (5%) | $45K | $57K | $55K | $157K |
| Contingency (5%) | $45K | $57K | $55K | $157K |
| **TOTAL** | **~$0.99M** | **~$1.24M** | **~$1.20M** | **~$3.43M** |

Year 1 sits cleanly under the $1M soft ceiling. Years 2 and 3 each run a little above it — Y2 because of the European exchange line items, Y3 because of journal production + 7 community launches. Both can be trimmed back under $1M flat if Minderoo wants the cap held hard, at the cost of either fewer European travellers, a thinner final book, or smaller community launches.

Funded by Minderoo as catalytic capital. Their legacy.

**The ask:** ~$3.43M over three years, with annual flow of ~$1.0M / $1.24M / $1.20M. Tight ops + contingency (5% each) — held there because the program design is conservative and the partner relationships are already in place.

**For context:** detaining one child for 3 years costs $3.9M. **Staying runs for less than the cost of detaining a single child**, reaches ~50 young people across 7 communities, sends 14 people to Europe and brings Europe back, and produces the largest community-led youth justice evidence base ever assembled in this country.

**What was cut to fit the envelope** (kept here so the conversation about scope is honest):

- Team from 2 FTE + 1 support → 1 FTE + 1 support
- Cadence from 6/6 → 4/8
- Year 2 from year-long European residency → distributed short exchange visits
- Journal from three chapter deliveries → one Year 3 delivery
- Year 3 national gallery tour → deferred to a Year 4 stretch goal raised separately

## The 7 communities — first-pass shortlist

| State | Likely candidate | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **NT** | [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] (Mparntwe) — Aunty Bev, Tanya Turner, Kristy Bloomfield | Existing partnership, very strong |
| **QLD (north)** | [[picc|PICC]] (Palm Island) — Richard Cassidy and the Bwgcolman families | Existing partnership |
| **QLD (Brisbane region)** | One of three candidates: **EPIC Pathways** (Rhian Miller), the **MMEIZC** team on Stradbroke Island (Minjerribah), or the **Toowoomba** team | Three-way pick — close-to-home community |
| **NSW** | Maranguka (Bourke Tribal Council) | Need to approach |
| **WA** | Olabud Doogethu (Halls Creek) | Need to approach |
| **TAS** | Prevention Not Detention (Loic Fery's coalition) | Pipeline contact |
| **VIC** | ??? | **OPEN — Q12** |
| **SA** | ??? | **OPEN — Q12** |

**How we find the 7 (locked):** there is no funnel. We start with the people we already know and trust — co-selecting alongside Minderoo and other aligned funders — and from there we radiate outward through trust, recommendation, and openness. New communities surface through search, peer recommendation, and open ideas, not through an application form. The filter is relationship, not process.

## Cultural protocol (non-negotiable)

1. No community is approached without prior consultation with existing ACT relationships in that region
2. **Elder and Council sign-off** before any photographs, recordings, or journals begin
3. **OCAP/CARE protocols** at the data layer via [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — the legal and technical baseline, not aspirational
4. **Young person owns their journal.** Right of withdrawal at any point, including post-exhibition; portraits and entries removed within 7 days of request
5. **Subjects under 18** require guardian and cultural authority sign-off
6. **Cultural review fees** are budgeted as line items, not absorbed as goodwill labour
7. **No exhibition opens** without at least one young person or cultural representative present
8. **Income from book/exhibition sales** flows on a published transparent split to subjects and their nominated community organisations

The first consent conversation matters more than the first photograph. Get the protocol wrong and the program should not exist.

## How it connects to the rest of ACT

- [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] — Staying is the field arm; JusticeHub is the world model that holds the evidence, ALMA is the data spine
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — every voice transcript, every consent, every story is captured here. The ethical and technical base.
- [[the-brave-ones|The Brave Ones]] — the visual discipline; every Staying portrait sits in the Brave Ones series
- [[contained|CONTAINED]] — companion piece; the touring exhibition travels alongside CONTAINED where it can
- [[diagrama|Diagrama]] — Year 2 partner; the international comparator
- [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] — first locked community partnership
- [[picc|Palm Island Community Company]] — second locked community partnership
- [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]] — Listen (Y1) → Compare ≈ Curiosity (Y2) → Tell ≈ Action + Art (Y3)
- [[third-reality|The Third Reality]] — the methodology Staying enacts at scale
- [[the-edge-is-where-the-healing-is-justicehub-as-the-world-model-for-community-led|The Edge Is Where the Healing Is]] — the synthesis this program operationalises

## Funding pathway

**Lead funder (proposed):** Minderoo Foundation — Walk Free + Generation One alignment, capacity for catalytic 3-year capital, international ambition matches the Year 2 European exchange.

**Contact:** Lucy Stronach (Minderoo). Already warm. Already asking for specific dollar numbers and plans.

**Approach (locked): return pitch with a tight envelope.** A previous ~$8M / 3-year shape was too much. The next pitch goes back at **~$3.43M total**, structured as ~$1M / $1.24M / $1.20M annual flow. Year 1 sits inside the soft ~$1M ceiling Lucy signalled; Years 2 and 3 each run ~$200–240K above it because that's where the European exchange and the journal/launches land. This is the shape that makes the program *move* rather than stall (see Budget envelope above).

The *Edge Holds* blog + LinkedIn piece still publish — but as accompaniment around the return pitch, not as a cold-warmup.

**Naming opportunity:** *"The Minderoo Australian Justice Cohort"* — international civic-infrastructure legacy positioning that a foundation will pay a premium for.

## Decisions locked (2026-04-08)

Q11–Q15 resolved in session:

- **Q11 — Year 2 is a distributed European exchange.** Each of the 7 communities sends 2 people (1 young person + 1 support) to *one* country: Spain (Diagrama), Holland (Halt), or Scotland (Children's Hearings). Focused short visits, not a year-long residency. Reciprocal European visits to Australia in the same year. Designed to make every community an international peer at a fraction of the year-long-team-in-residence cost.
- **Q12 — Brisbane region community is a three-way pick** between EPIC Pathways (Rhian Miller), the MMEIZC team on Stradbroke Island (Minjerribah), and the Toowoomba team. VIC and SA candidates still to be sourced through trust-based outreach (not a public call).
- **Q13 — No 30 → 7 funnel.** Co-select with Minderoo and other aligned funders starting from the people we already know and trust, then radiate outward through trust, recommendation, and openness. No application form. The filter is relationship.
- **Q14 — Communities first.** Year 3 produces seven community-led launches in the seven places, plus a published book that gathers the seven journals (with consent) into one volume. The national gallery tour (NGA / MCA / NGV) is **deferred to a Year-4 stretch goal** raised separately — outside this $3.43M envelope.
- **Q15 — Return pitch with a tight envelope.** Lucy Stronach is already warm and asking for numbers. A prior ~$8M shape was too much. New shape: **~$3.43M total** at ~$1M / $1.24M / $1.20M annual flow. Y1 inside the soft $1M ceiling, Y2/Y3 a touch above to carry Europe and book production. The program is re-cut (1 FTE + 1 support, distributed European exchange, journal as Y3 delivery) to fit. *Edge Holds* publishes alongside the pitch, not as cold warmup.

## LCAA Phase

In the [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]], Staying *is* the methodology — the wiki backlink names the mapping directly: *"Listen (Y1) → Compare ≈ Curiosity (Y2) → Tell ≈ Action + Art (Y3)."* The three-act structure of the program (Listen / Compare / Tell) is the LCAA arc made operational across three years and seven communities.

LCAA arc for Staying:
- **Listen — Year 1 (4 months on, 8 months virtual)** — small team rotates through 7 communities; deep accompaniment without arrival-and-departure; the team that *stays* through the season the program is ostensibly about
- **Curiosity — Year 2 European exchange** — each community sends 2 travellers (1 young person + 1 support) to one of [[diagrama|Diagrama]] (Spain), Halt (Holland), or Children's Hearings (Scotland); reciprocal European visits to Australia in the same year; *"those conversations have never happened in this country's history"*
- **Action — Year 3 community-led launches** — seven launches in seven places; a national published book gathering the seven journals (with consent) into one volume; a copy to every electorate office
- **Art — the per-young-person Journal** — A5, hand-stitched, ~80–120 pages, owned by the young person, in [[the-brave-ones|Brave Ones]] visual discipline; *if the program produces nothing else, the journals are the proof*

Cultural protocol is the gate: Elder and Council sign-off before any photographs, recordings, or journals begin; OCAP/CARE protocols at the data layer via [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]]; the first consent conversation matters more than the first photograph.

Staying is the *methodology layer* of [[three-circles|The Three Circles]] Circle Two — not a competing pitch.

pages.content:
> Two cabins, 150 acres of Jinibara Country, and room to be quiet. The Pink Cabin and the Train Carriage are bookable directly. This is the self-guided end of the farm — you're on the land, we're light-touch hosts.

**Status:** Active | **Code:** ACT-FM-EXP-stays | **Cluster:** [[act-farm|ACT Farm]]

## What it is

We offer direct-book accommodation at [[black-cockatoo-valley|Black Cockatoo Valley]] — the Pink Cabin and the Train Carriage. Unlike the rest of the experiences in this catalog, stays are instant-book, not inquiry-based. You pick your dates, pay the deposit, and we confirm.

Stays are deliberately simple. You're not signing up for a program. You're renting a cabin on a working land-practice and spending time with the place. We ask you to respect conservation boundaries we explain on arrival and otherwise leave you alone.

## Who it's for

- Writers, artists, and practitioners wanting quiet work time
- Couples and small families wanting a weekend on Country
- Locals from the hinterland who want a night away without the drive
- People scoping a longer engagement (residency, retreat) who want to see the place first

## What happens

Not much, by design. You arrive, we do a brief walk-around, and then the cabin is yours. Linen, kitchen basics, firewood in season. Optional: garden access, walking tracks, and — if you're here at the right time — a [[the-harvest|Harvest]] breakfast in Witta on the weekend.

We don't run a program around stays. If you want more — a workshop, a residency, a retreat — we have other offers for that.

## Price, duration, capacity

| Item | Detail |
|------|--------|
| **Duration** | 2-night minimum |
| **Capacity** | Pink Cabin and Train Carriage each sleep 2; Pink Cabin has capacity for a small family on request |
| **Price** | Pink Cabin **$210/night** · Train Carriage **$190/night** · $45 cleaning fee · 2-night minimum |
| **Includes** | Linen, kitchen basics, tea and coffee, firewood (seasonal), land access |
| **Doesn't include** | Meals (self-catered), transport |
| **Season** | Year-round |

## Booking

Direct-book. Available on the ACT Farm site at `/stay` with per-cabin pages at `/stay/pink-cabin` and `/stay/train-carriage`. We process bookings through the site and confirm within one working day. You'll get a `BCV-XXXXX` reference number at the booking step.

pages.title: Storytelling, Data Sovereignty, and Community Recovery
pages.excerpt: Storytelling and data sovereignty anchor recovery work, with Elders guiding what is shared and why.
pages.content:
> Storytelling and data sovereignty anchor recovery work, with Elders guiding what is shared and why.

## Context

**Place:** Palm Island community
**Voice Owner:** Community storytellers and Elders group (consented)
**Consent Status:** EXTERNAL-LITE — Elders review required for external use

## Story

In the aftermath of devastating storms, Palm Island community faced not just physical recovery but the challenge of telling their own story. Previous disaster responses had seen external media and researchers arrive, extract stories, and leave — sometimes misrepresenting the community or exposing sensitive information.

Through Empathy Ledger, the community established a different model. Elders guide what is shared and why. Storytellers maintain control over their narratives. Data sovereignty means the community owns their recovery story.

The result: recovery documentation that serves the community first, respects cultural protocols, and provides evidence for future planning — on the community's terms.

## ALMA Signals

| Signal | Level | Notes |
|--------|-------|-------|
| **Authority** | High | Elder guidance, community control |
| **Evidence** | High | Narrative documentation of recovery |
| **Harm Risk** | Medium | Storm impacts are sensitive |
| **Capability** | Medium | Ongoing, building capacity |
| **Option Value** | High | Model for future recovery |
| **Community Value Return** | High | Community owns the narrative |

## Connections

**LCAA Shift:** Listen (gathering storm impact stories) → Art (story becomes shared recovery practice). Storytelling became infrastructure for community-led recovery, not external extraction.

*Consent reviewed: 2025-12 | Next review: 2026-06*

pages.title: Strategic Decisions Log
pages.excerpt: The load-bearing decisions that shape ACT's strategy. Distilled from 58 decision records in project_knowledge, filtered down to the dozen that matter most.
pages.content:
> The load-bearing decisions that shape ACT's strategy. Distilled from 58 decision records in `project_knowledge`, filtered down to the dozen that matter most.

## Why a Curated Log

Of the 58 decisions stored in Supabase, most are routine student-team meeting choices from 2023–2024 development sprints (`ACT-MISC` code). The decisions below are the genuinely strategic ones — the moments where ACT chose a direction, refused a path, or framed a problem in a way that changed downstream work.

## 2026

### Founder Lanes + Top Two Bets (2026-04-10, ACT-HQ)

**Decision:** Benjamin focuses on product, infrastructure, positioning, and paid pilots. Nicholas focuses on relationships, field practice, art, and place-based pull. ACT narrows its drive lane to two flagship bets: [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] and [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] + [[civicgraph|CivicGraph]] treated as one stack. [[contained|CONTAINED]] remains the campaign front door, not a separate third flagship.

**Why it matters:** This is the first explicit founder-level portfolio cut made against ACT's own PTO discipline. It addresses three recurring problems at once: too many active projects, Benjamin as technical bottleneck, and a drift toward bespoke support work that does not compound. The full rationale and proof lines live in [[2026-04-founder-lanes-and-top-two-bets|the dated decision note]].

### PRF Power Analysis: 61/22/17 Split (2026-03-26, ACT-HQ)

Of ~$90M in traceable Paul Ramsay Foundation grants:
- **61%** → universities + large intermediaries
- **22%** → community organisations
- **17%** → ACCOs directly (only 1 of top 10 grants — Anindilyakwa $3.45M)
- **ACF** intermediates $17.6M+
- PRF claims 50%+ First Nations support, but that's strategy-aligned only — actual $220M Indigenous work = 19% of $1.15B total
- Revenue source: Ramsay Health Care dividends (PRF holds 17.58% stake)

**Why it matters:** The Kristy Muir Power letter (Feb 2026) was a genuine signal of intent, but structural inertia in PRF's grant-making means most dollars still flow upstream. This analysis is the basis for ACT's 2026 funder engagement strategy: don't pitch PRF as a transactional funder; pitch them on the structural problem their own data reveals.

### PLACE as JusticeHub Entry Point (2026-03-26, ACT-HQ)

PLACE Network (Dr Luke Craven, CEO) connects every target funder ACT cares about — PRF, Dusseldorp, Minderoo, Ian Potter, Bryan, AusGov — and has no data platform of its own. Ian Trust bridges PLACE Community Council and PRF FNAC. Tennant Creek (Oonchiumpa basecamp) is in the SPSP network.

**Decision:** Position [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] as the evidence platform PLACE communities need, not as a competing initiative. Entry through Luke Craven (systems-change practitioner who will immediately understand the value proposition) rather than through traditional foundation-relations channels.

### Westpac Event 30 March (2026-03-27, ACT-HV)

**Decision:** Proceed with Westpac event on 30 March.
**Rationale:** Align with Mounty visit and Jo's attendance.
**Source:** NM/BK sync.

A small operational decision, included here because it represents the cadence of opportunistic stakeholder alignment that drives ACT's relationship-building rhythm.

## 2025

### Spain Trip — Diagrama Engagement (2025-01-16, ACT-DG)

**Decision:** Move forward with planning the Spain trip.
**Rationale:** Engage high-profile decision-makers in understanding [[diagrama|Diagrama]]'s approach to youth justice.

This is the decision that produced the 2025 Spain delegation and the foundation for ACT's [[global-precedents|global precedents]] research thread. Without this trip, the Diagrama partnership stays theoretical.

## 2024

### Reject the Loan (2024-11-07, ACT-DG)

**Decision:** Do not pursue a loan.
**Rationale:** Preference for support from the UK instead.

A small decision with implications: ACT chose relational capital over debt, even when a loan was available. This pattern (prefer aligned capital over neutral capital) recurs across 2025–2026 funding decisions.

### YJ Legislative Push (2024-05-22, ACT-DG)

**Decision:** Pursue legislative changes for youth justice.
**Rationale:** Improve the system based on experiences from Spain.

The genesis decision for ACT's [[youth-justice-reform|youth justice reform]] advocacy posture — shifting from program delivery to systems change.

## 2023

### Central Tech Platform (2023-05-29, ACT-JH)

**Decision:** Develop a central technology platform to support individual agency and data control.
**Rationale:** Enable better integration and user experience in the human services system.
**Source:** TYSON Bank workshop.

**This is the genesis decision for what became [[justicehub|JusticeHub]].** Everything downstream — ALMA, the intervention portfolio, the funding landscape work — traces to this single sentence.

### ACT Supports Confit Pathways (2023-03-29, ACT-EL)

**Decision:** A Curious Tractor will support the pitch and build of the Confit Pathways application.
**Rationale:** Address pain points in scaling the program and enhance community support.

The first formal commitment to the [[confit-pathways|Confit Pathways]] partnership — a pattern ACT would repeat: take responsibility for the technology layer of someone else's mission rather than running parallel programs.

## What's NOT in this Log

The 58 raw decision records also include:
- 30+ student team operational decisions (Notion vs Miro, IntelliJ vs other IDEs, MySQL vs other databases)
- A handful of meeting cadence decisions
- Form-design choices for early app prototypes

These are preserved in the raw snapshot at `wiki/raw/2026-04-07-supabase-strategic-decisions-snapshot.md` for completeness, but they don't belong in the strategic narrative.

## Backlinks

- [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] — central to most strategic decisions above
- [[diagrama|Diagrama]] — Spain trip decisions
- [[power-dynamics-philanthropy|Power Dynamics in Philanthropy]] — context for the PRF analysis
- [[roadmap-2026|Roadmap 2026]] — what these decisions are now executing toward
- [[funding-transparency|Funding Transparency]] — the philosophical thread

pages.title: Studio Business Model
pages.excerpt: The Studio does not need to behave like a SaaS business, but it does need a clear economic logic. The point is to fund the commons, deepen the field, and keep artistic work strategically alive.
pages.content:
> The Studio does not need to behave like a SaaS business, but it does need a clear economic logic. The point is to fund the commons, deepen the field, and keep artistic work strategically alive.

## The Core Principle

ACT's art field is not valuable only if it sells objects.

The Studio's business model is a mixed model. It creates value through:

- direct revenue
- strategic leverage
- ecosystem strengthening
- documentation and syndication
- new partnership pathways

Success is therefore broader than "sold more works this quarter," but it still has to be legible in practical terms.

## Revenue Pathways

### 1. Touring and licensing

Some works behave like deployable public infrastructure.

Example:
- [[contained|CONTAINED]] can tour, be hosted, and be licensed into institutional or public contexts

This pathway can generate:

- venue fees
- touring fees
- facilitation fees
- documentation fees

### 2. Commissions

ACT can be commissioned to create works for:

- public institutions
- conferences
- cultural organisations
- councils
- community partners
- justice and social innovation settings

The right commission is one that strengthens the field, not just the invoice line.

Projects like [[gold-phone|Gold.Phone]] also point toward a hostable communication-installation format, while [[cars-and-microcontrollers|Cars and Microcontrollers]] points toward education, workshop, and maker-lab pathways that still sit inside the Studio logic rather than outside it.
[[the-confessional|The Confessional]] also sits here as a mobile therapeutic-art format that could be hosted or commissioned into remote and underserved contexts without losing its artistic logic.

### 3. Residencies and fellowships

The Studio can earn through:

- artist residencies
- research residencies
- field labs
- regional fellowships

These can link strongly to [[black-cockatoo-valley|Black Cockatoo Valley]] and [[the-harvest|The Harvest]].
This is the logic behind [[regional-arts-fellowship|Regional Arts Fellowship]] — not as a side program, but as one of the repeatable ways the Studio can support regional practice and earn while deepening the field.

### 4. Artwork sales and editions

Some pieces or derivative outputs can generate revenue through:

- original artwork sales
- editions
- prints
- objects
- documentation artefacts

This matters especially where cultural authority and artist value need to stay visible, as with [[uncle-allan-palm-island-art|Uncle Allan Palm Island Art]].

### 5. Strategic spillover

The Studio also creates downstream revenue by strengthening:

- ACT's public identity
- project trust and visibility
- partner confidence
- future commissions
- grant narratives
- ecosystem ventures

This spillover is real and should be named, even when it is not booked as "art revenue."

## What Success Looks Like

The Studio succeeds when it is strong across four dimensions.

### Artistic success

- the works are coherent, memorable, and publicly legible
- the Studio line feels like a real body of work, not disconnected outputs

### Strategic success

- works strengthen ACT's wider ecosystem arguments
- works open conversations that policy or products alone cannot open
- works bring the right people into the field

### Economic success

- works generate earned income through touring, commissions, residencies, sales, or licensing
- the Studio is not permanently dependent on grant subsidy alone
- revenue helps sustain ACT's wider commons and cultural production

### Ecosystem success

- EL gains stronger photo/video/story material
- the websites gain stronger public surfaces
- flagship projects gain cultural depth
- ACT's philosophy becomes easier to communicate through public work

## How To Measure It

The Studio should track a blend of:

- hosted works / tours / placements
- commission value
- residency and fellowship income
- artwork / edition sales
- media and story assets captured in [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]]
- partner enquiries and repeat hosts
- related ecosystem outcomes opened by the work

## What Not To Do

The Studio should avoid:

- flattening every work into a product pitch
- chasing commissions that weaken the field
- treating strategic spillover as an excuse for having no revenue logic
- separating art from community, place, and ecosystem context

## Website Implication

The website should help the business model, not hide it.

That means the `Works` layer should be able to show:

- what the work is
- how it can be hosted, commissioned, or toured
- how it links to a broader ACT field
- enough photo/video/story evidence to make that invitation real

pages.title: Studio Innovation Flow
pages.excerpt: The Studio is where ACT tests public feeling, strategic framing, and material form before those ideas harden into systems, campaigns, or enterprises.
pages.content:
> The Studio is where ACT tests public feeling, strategic framing, and material form before those ideas harden into systems, campaigns, or enterprises.

## The Role Of The Studio

The Studio is not just an output channel. It is part of ACT's innovation engine.

It does at least four kinds of work:

1. **Prototype public arguments**
2. **Translate ecosystem learning into form**
3. **Create new relationships and invitations**
4. **Generate proof that can flow back into products, campaigns, and strategy**

## The Flow

### 1. Pressure enters through the field

Pressure comes from:

- Country and place
- community relationships
- policy failures
- bureaucratic absurdity
- stories and testimony
- product and service gaps

This is the `Listen` and `Curiosity` phase.

### 2. The Studio shapes a work

A work takes that pressure and turns it into:

- an installation
- an object
- a room
- a vehicle
- a sound piece
- a communications intervention

The work is the prototype of a public argument.

### 3. The work creates response

A strong work creates:

- public attention
- emotional understanding
- documentation
- media
- invitations
- partner conversations
- new stories

This is where the Studio becomes strategic rather than decorative.

### 4. Response feeds the ecosystem back

That response can strengthen:

- [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] — by making its evidence felt
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — by generating live story, media, and voice
- [[goods-on-country|Goods on Country]] — by showing practical innovation in real communities
- [[the-harvest|The Harvest]] and [[black-cockatoo-valley|Black Cockatoo Valley]] — by bringing residencies, gatherings, and documentation into place
- ACT's public site — by giving the ecosystem a strong cultural and visual identity

## Innovation Types

### Strategic innovation

Works change how people understand a problem.

Example:
- [[contained|CONTAINED]] turns justice reform from abstract evidence into a direct felt comparison.
- [[the-confessional|The Confessional]] turns care and vulnerability into a mobile public encounter rather than a service brochure.

### Cultural innovation

Works change what kinds of stories and presences are possible in public.

Example:
- [[uncle-allan-palm-island-art|Uncle Allan Palm Island Art]]
- [[gold-phone|Gold.Phone]]
- [[treacher|Treacher]]

### Material innovation

Works reveal new formats, objects, or interfaces that can flow back into enterprise or product thinking.

Example:
- [[the-caravan|The Caravan]] as mobile infrastructure
- [[cars-and-microcontrollers|Cars and Microcontrollers]] as a maker pathway where practical intelligence becomes technical confidence
- the installation logic across the Studio line as a repeatable deployment pattern

### Relational innovation

Works create the conditions for new collaborators, hosts, funders, commissioners, and communities to enter the field.

Example:
- [[regional-arts-fellowship|Regional Arts Fellowship]] as a support structure for practitioners who otherwise fall between art, agtech, and land practice categories

## Strategic Flow For The Website

The website should reflect this flow directly:

- the wiki explains the durable meaning of the work
- EL carries the live media, stories, and documentation
- the website shows the work as part of the ecosystem's strategic movement

That means a work page should not just say what the piece is. It should help show:

- what field pressure produced it
- what public argument it carries
- what projects it strengthens
- what invitations it opens

## What The Studio Produces Beyond Art

The Studio does not only produce artworks. It also produces:

- field language
- campaign energy
- partner confidence
- public identity
- documentation assets
- future ventures

That is why art belongs near the centre of ACT's innovation model.

pages.title: The Aesthetics of Asymmetry
pages.excerpt: An art project about what happens when public systems become visible. Six episodes, one living data organism. April–September 2026.
pages.content:
> *An art project about what happens when public systems become visible. Six episodes, one living data organism. April–September 2026.*

## What it is

A six-episode public art campaign that turns ACT's three platforms ([[civicgraph|CivicGraph]], [[justicehub|JusticeHub]], [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]]) into a living data organism people can stand inside, argue with, and carry away as physical objects. Each episode sits in the lineage of institutional critique (Hans Haacke, Mark Lombardi, Forensic Architecture), digital-age visibility politics (Hito Steyerl, Hasan Elahi, Mimi Onuoha), and Indigenous data sovereignty (Maiam nayri Wingara, CARE principles).

It is also quietly the marketing layer for a real commercial arm: CivicGraph subscriptions, JusticeHub evidence queries, and Empathy Ledger syndication all sit one click below the art. The campaign's thesis is that the art is the marketing — and the marketing is honest because the platforms already do what they claim.

## The six episodes

| #   | Slug                               | Status                     | After               | One-line                                                        |                                                                          |
| --- | ---------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 01  | [[episode-01-keyhole               | The Keyhole]]              | LIVE · April 2026   | James C. Scott                                                  | What the applicant sees, what the funder sees, the distance between them |
| 02  | Resolution                         | Building · May 2026        | Hito Steyerl        | Clarity can be care. Clarity can be capture. The pixel decides. |                                                                          |
| 03  | The Missing Folder                 | Scheduled · June 2026      | Mimi Onuoha         | 873 postcodes where absence is the subject                      |                                                                          |
| 04  | The Promise and the Purchase Order | Scheduled · July 2026      | —                   | Hansard vs the money trail                                      |                                                                          |
| 05  | The Alibi                          | Scheduled · August 2026    | Hasan Elahi         | Total transparency as concealment                               |                                                                          |
| 06  | CARE                               | Scheduled · September 2026 | Maiam nayri Wingara | Consent is the only honest transparency                         |                                                                          |

## How it connects to the ecosystem

- **[[civicgraph|CivicGraph]]** — the systemic data layer. Public records joined by ABN: 587K entities, 1.5M relationships, $74B in contracts, 301K political donations, 30K grants. The art pulls live from GrantScope's public `/api/data/*` endpoints.
- **[[justicehub|JusticeHub]]** — the evidence layer. 1,775 community-led programs, 128 verified top-tier. The art links to JusticeHub's program search wherever a viewer wants to know "what works, where?"
- **[[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]]** — the narrative sovereignty layer. 226 consent-governed storytellers. The campaign registers a new `syndication_site` in EL v2 and pulls consented content (quotes, portraits, transcripts) via the public `/api/syndication/justicehub/*` pattern. Registration steps live in `act-aesthetics-of-asymmetry/OPERATOR_NOTES.md`.

## Technical architecture

A separate Next.js 15 app at `aesthetics.act.place` (currently developed at `/Users/benknight/Code/act-aesthetics-of-asymmetry`). Consumes GrantScope public APIs and a new EL v2 site-scoped API. Uses:

- `@cosmos.gl/graph` — GPU force graph at 500K+ nodes
- `sigma` + `graphology` — curated sub-views
- `deck.gl` + `mapbox-gl` — funding deserts, flows by geography
- `p5` + `three` — organic motion, GLSL aesthetics
- `scrollama` + `gsap` — scrollytelling

See [[what-is-the-living-organism-the-visual-system-for-the-aesthetics-of-asymmetry|the Living Organism synthesis]] for the full spec.

## Brand system

Austere / confrontational. Bauhaus reference points: font-black uppercase display, monospace data, 4px heavy borders. Palette locked to near-black `#0A0A0A`, bone cream `#F5F5F0`, urgent red `#DC2626`, deep navy `#0A1628`. Typography: Archivo Black (display), Inter (body), JetBrains Mono (data).

This diverges deliberately from the [[visual-system|Red Centre]] paperback aesthetic that anchors ACT's other outputs. The campaign is asymmetric to the rest of the ecosystem in appearance — that is the point.

A fresh Pencil (`.pen`) design file will be created to house the emblem (filing-cabinet-with-glowing-empty-folder — Onuoha homage), poster templates, and social assets.

## Physical artifacts

Every episode ships with a printable artifact. Plotter-compatible SVG exports via p5-svg → AxiDraw. Riso colour separation for posters. QR codes on the back link to parameterised URLs (`/episode/keyhole?entity=<id>`) so a physical postcard opens a specific live view.

| Episode | Artifact |
|---|---|
| 01 Keyhole | A2 poster, keyhole die-cut, 2-colour Riso |
| 02 Resolution | AxiDraw 6-panel gradient print |
| 03 Missing Folder | Screen-printed manila-folder set |
| 04 Promise / Purchase Order | A1 broadsheet foldout |
| 05 Alibi | Personalised foldout poster |
| 06 CARE | QR postcard to EL storyteller audio |

## Narrative store

Campaign claims live in [wiki/narrative/civicgraph/](../../narrative/civicgraph/INDEX.md). Each LinkedIn post, pitch, or press piece deploys a specific claim and is logged via `narrative-log-deployment.mjs`. Frames in rotation: structural, confrontational, evidentiary, testimonial, invitational, constructive, art.

pages.title: The Brave Ones
pages.excerpt: Real portraits. Real stories. Real young people. The ones changing the system.
pages.content:
> Real portraits. Real stories. Real young people. The ones changing the system.

**Status:** Ideation (sketched 2026-04-07) | **Cluster:** Art (Studio) | **Tier:** Studio piece in development

## Overview

The Brave Ones is a sustained photographic and storytelling series sitting in the [[act-studio|ACT Studio cluster]] alongside [[contained|CONTAINED]]. Where CONTAINED puts you inside the *room* that youth detention is, The Brave Ones puts you in front of the *people* who walked out the other side. It is the deliberate counter-mugshot: studio-quality B&W portraits in the dignity register that policing and media have refused to give Indigenous and system-impacted young people for two centuries.

It is also the visual architecture of [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] — the human face of the world model — and the answer to the photo-credit problem every justice org runs into: the entire image library for the next decade of community-led justice work in Australia, with consent built in at the layer below.

## Cluster Context

The Brave Ones is a work-series inside the [[projects/justicehub/README|JusticeHub Cluster]], not a disconnected studio side project. The wiki should hold the philosophy, protocol, and role of the series in the justice constellation, [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] should hold the portraits, permissions, voice fragments, and future galleries, and the websites should compose those layers through the [[../../technical/wiki-project-and-work-sync-contract|Wiki Project and Work Sync Contract]] and [[../../concepts/living-website-operating-system|Living Website Operating System]].

## Why this exists

A diagram is read once and filed. A portrait is stood in front of. The CONTAINED tour proved that the move that breaks a funder, a judge, or a minister is not a stat — it is a body in a room. The Brave Ones is that move at scale and on repeat. It is also self-replicating: every new portrait is a new ALMA node, a new [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] story, a new Tractorpedia article. The system gets smarter every time someone stands in front of the lens.

The name does the inversion in three words. The dominant media calls these young people "at-risk youth", "offenders", "system-impacted". The Brave Ones says: *they are not the problem. They are the proof. And they are braver than anyone in the system that failed them.*

## Visual language

The reference is the Brian Duffy / *Station to Station*-era David Bowie portrait register, 1976:

- High-contrast black & white, soft halated key light from a single source
- Deep velvety blacks, silvery mid-tones, almost no pure whites except in the halation
- Film grain texture — never digital crispness
- Shallow depth of field, subject emerging from shadow
- Devotional close framing — chin/hand/contemplation
- Refuses the colour-coded infographic vocabulary of every other systems-change visual
- Negative space carries weight

Palette: bone white (#F4F0E8) and velvet black (#0E0E10). Optional single accent: blood ochre (#7A2F1A), used at most once per artefact.

Typography: refined serif, set small, set far from the centre. Numbers and statistics never appear on the portrait — they live in companion artefacts. The image is the argument; the data is the evidence.

## Components

| Layer | What it is | Who holds it |
|---|---|---|
| The portraits | Studio-quality B&W photographs, single visual continuity, life-size when printed | The photographer + each subject's editorial control |
| The voices | Each portrait paired with the young person's own words, captured via Empathy Ledger, transcribed verbatim | Empathy Ledger consent layer |
| The stories | One-page case study per portrait: where they were, what changed, who held them | JusticeHub + community partner |
| The cohort | The young people in the series form a real cohort — they meet, mentor each other, speak together, become a constituency | The young people themselves |
| The galleries | A touring physical exhibition — MCA, NGV, Powerhouse, regional galleries, ACCO halls, parliament foyers | ACT Studio + venue partners |
| The online hall | A permanent presence on JusticeHub — each portrait a node in ALMA | JusticeHub + Empathy Ledger |
| The book | Year three: the printed book | ACT publishing partner |

## The trace layer

If JusticeHub is going to improve responsibly, it needs more than quantitative traces like search logs, funding rows, and QR scans. It also needs durable qualitative traces that explain what actually changed in the room.

That is one of The Brave Ones' most important jobs. The portraits, paired words, and consented follow-up reflections are not decorative brand assets. They are the trace layer that stops JusticeHub from optimising toward sterile dashboards. They let ACT ask not just *did this convert?* but *what did the judge see, what made the funder pause, and what felt true enough to move money or practice?*

The portraits themselves are not the thing to auto-optimise. The editable surfaces are the surrounding harnesses: exhibition sequencing, caption scaffolds, invitation flow, and the way the work hands off into [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] and [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]]. The longer articulation is filed at [[how-should-act-apply-the-karpathy-loop-to-justicehub-the-minderoo-pitch-and-the-|Karpathy loop alignment synthesis]].

## Cultural protocol (non-negotiable)

Before a single Indigenous young person sits for a portrait:

1. **Aunty Bev, Uncle Terry, Tanya Turner, Kristy Bloomfield** at [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] are consulted and the protocol is co-designed
2. **Empathy Ledger consent flow** is the legal and technical baseline — not aspirational
3. **Each subject has right of withdrawal at any point**, including after exhibition; portraits removed from all venues and digital instances within 7 days of request
4. **Subjects under 18** require guardian and cultural authority sign-off
5. **No exhibition opens without at least one subject (or a designated cultural representative) present** — this is their show, not ours
6. **Income** from commercial use (print sales, book sales, licensing) flows to subjects and their nominated community organisations on a transparent published split

The first consent conversation is more important than the first photograph. If we get the protocol wrong, the project should not exist.

## Phase plan

| Phase | Time | Cohort | Key activity | Cost (rough) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0. Placeholder** | This week | 1 stand-in image | Three Ripples poster, Minderoo deck, internal review | $0 |
| **1. Pilot** | Months 1–3 | 5 young people | First proper sittings (Mparntwe, Bourke, one other), consent flow tested end-to-end | ~$15K |
| **2. Launch** | Months 3–12 | 25 young people | First public gallery exhibition. JusticeHub homepage relaunched around the series. | ~$80K |
| **3. National tour** | Months 12–24 | 100 portraits | Travels alongside CONTAINED. Book published. Every electorate office. | ~$200K |
| **4. Annual** | Ongoing | +20–30/year | The series becomes a fixture of Australian civic life | ~$50K/year |

## Funding pathway

This is catalytic philanthropic capital with art-grant compatibility. Likely funders:

- **Minderoo Foundation** — Walk Free + Generation One justice alignment
- **Vincent Fairfax Family Foundation** — has funded portrait series before
- **Lord Mayor's Charitable Foundation** — Melbourne arts + justice crossover
- **Ian Potter Foundation** — community-led arts
- **Australia Council / Creative Australia** — direct arts grant pathway
- **R&D Tax** — photography, consent-tech, and platform work all eligible under ACT's existing R&D incentive claim

Lead-funder naming opportunity: *"The [Funder Name] Brave Ones Portrait Series"* — civic-infrastructure legacy positioning a foundation will pay a premium for.

## How it connects to the rest of ACT

- [[justicehub|JusticeHub]] — each portrait becomes a node in ALMA; the series is the human face of the data layer
- [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — consent + sovereignty + voice capture; the technical and ethical base
- [[contained|CONTAINED]] — companion piece; portraits live on the inside walls of the rooms
- [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] — likely first community partnership; cultural protocol design
- [[picc|Palm Island Community Company]] — second community partnership; longitudinal subjects
- [[third-reality|The Third Reality]] — the methodology this series operationalises
- [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]] — Art (the fourth letter); the form that completes Listen → Curiosity → Action

## Stories already in the wiki worth photographing

These are the young people whose stories are already documented and consented at some level via [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] — the natural seed cohort:

- **Xavier** (Oonchiumpa) — built the Stretch Bed; was told by formal reports he had "limited ability to understand"; Oonchiumpa bet on his version
- **MS** (Oonchiumpa) — thought he was from Alice Springs; reconnected with family across Central Australia; building a tourism venture on his own Country
- **CB** (Oonchiumpa) — becoming a man, becoming a leader in Town Camp
- **Jackqwann** (Mparntwe) — rapper exploring identity, cultural heritage, belonging
- **A** (Oonchiumpa) — guarded to self-advocate after losing her mother
- **M** (Oonchiumpa) — homelessness to independent living
- **L** (Oonchiumpa, age 16) — named the cause of youth incarceration in one word: *"Oppression."*

Plus subjects to be drawn from Maranguka (Bourke), [[picc|Palm Island]], and [[confit-pathways|Confit Pathways]] as the cohort expands.

## First move (this week)

Use a **placeholder portrait** for the Three Ripples poster — pulled from Empathy Ledger's already-consented archive OR a public-domain reference image clearly marked as a stand-in. The placeholder lets us prove the visual concept this week, brief the photographer with an actual mockup, and share the framing internally (Aunty Bev, Tanya Turner, Brodie, Joe Kwon) for cultural feedback *before* any young person sits.

The placeholder is explicitly labelled as a stand-in everywhere it appears, and is replaced the moment Phase 1 portraits are shot.

## LCAA Phase

In the [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]], The Brave Ones sits squarely in the **Art** phase — the wiki backlink already names it: *"Art (the fourth letter); the form that completes Listen → Curiosity → Action."* Where [[contained|CONTAINED]] puts you inside the *room* youth detention is, The Brave Ones puts you in front of the *people* who walked out the other side.

LCAA arc for The Brave Ones:
- **Listen** — every portrait is paired with the young person's own words, captured via [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] and transcribed verbatim; cultural protocol co-designed with Aunty Bev, Uncle Terry, Tanya Turner, and Kristy Bloomfield at [[oonchiumpa|Oonchiumpa]] before any sitting
- **Curiosity** — the inversion the title performs in three words: *they are not the problem. They are the proof. And they are braver than anyone in the system that failed them.*
- **Action** — Phase 1 pilot (5 portraits) → Launch (25 portraits + first gallery exhibition) → National tour with [[contained|CONTAINED]] (100 portraits + book) → Annual fixture (20–30/year ongoing); each portrait becomes a node in ALMA on [[justicehub|JusticeHub]]
- **Art** — studio-quality B&W portraits in the Brian Duffy / *Station to Station* register: bone white and velvet black, devotional close framing, the dignity register that policing and media have refused these young people for two centuries

A diagram is read once and filed; a portrait is stood in front of. The Brave Ones is the move that has broken funders, judges, and ministers in a CONTAINED room — at scale and on repeat.

## Backlinks

pages.title: The Buttery
pages.excerpt: The Buttery is a drug and alcohol rehabilitation and treatment service based in Bangalow, northern New South Wales. Founded in 1976, it is one of Australia's longest-running therapeutic communities.
pages.content:
> The Buttery is a drug and alcohol rehabilitation and treatment service based in Bangalow, northern New South Wales. Founded in 1976, it is one of Australia's longest-running therapeutic communities.

**Relationship to ACT:** The Buttery is one of four Y1 bespoke customers for [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]]'s Annual Field Service (alongside JCF, [[picc|PICC]], and [[smart-recovery|SMART Recovery]]), at roughly $50K annual engagement.

## What The Buttery Does

The Buttery operates residential rehabilitation programs for people experiencing drug and alcohol addiction, using the therapeutic community (TC) model. Residents live together in a structured, supportive environment where recovery happens through shared responsibility, mutual aid, and peer accountability rather than purely clinical intervention. Programs typically run 16 to 26 weeks.

The organisation also delivers non-residential services including day programs, family support, aftercare, and community outreach across the Northern Rivers region. It is a member of the Australasian Therapeutic Communities Association (ATCA).

## History

Founded in 1976 by a group of community members in the Byron Bay hinterland, The Buttery is one of Australia's oldest therapeutic communities. The name comes from the original property, a former dairy in Bangalow. For nearly fifty years it has operated continuously through shifting government policy, funding cycles, and public attitudes toward addiction, maintaining its founding commitment to community-based recovery.

The Buttery's longevity is itself evidence: a community-controlled model that has survived five decades of institutional pressure to centralise, medicalise, or defund residential rehabilitation.

## Why It Matters to ACT

The Buttery is a natural partner for [[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]] because recovery narratives are among the most powerful and most exploited stories in the social sector. People in residential rehab share deeply personal experiences of addiction, trauma, family breakdown, and transformation. Those stories are routinely extracted by funders, media, and government for reporting purposes, with little regard for the storyteller's ongoing consent or dignity.

Empathy Ledger's consent-governed storytelling infrastructure gives The Buttery's residents and alumni sovereign control over their recovery narratives. Stories can be shared, restricted, or withdrawn at any time. This is not a technology overlay on existing practice; it is the missing layer that makes ethical storytelling possible in a context where vulnerability is the baseline.

## Connections

- **[[smart-recovery|SMART Recovery]]** -- both organisations operate in the addiction and recovery space. SMART Recovery is another of Empathy Ledger's four Y1 bespoke customers, creating a natural cluster of consent-governed recovery storytelling across different treatment modalities.
- **[[empathy-ledger|Empathy Ledger]]** -- The Buttery is a Y1 bespoke customer. EL provides the sovereign storytelling layer for residents and alumni to own their recovery narratives.
- **[[justicehub|JusticeHub]]** -- many young people in the justice system have co-occurring substance issues. The Buttery's evidence base on residential rehabilitation outcomes feeds directly into JusticeHub's case for community-led alternatives to detention.
- **[[empathy-ledger/annual-field-service|EL Annual Field Service]]** -- the operational engagement model through which ACT delivers bespoke storytelling services to The Buttery.
- **[[art/y1-release-program|Y1 Art Release Program]]** -- two of the eight Y1 art releases centre on The Buttery: the *Fifty Years of Coming Home* anthology and the 50-year cinematic documentary.

## ACT Work in Progress

- **Fifty Years of Coming Home** -- 200-page hardcover anthology documenting The Buttery's 50-year history, interviews, archival photos, Paul Kelly connection, timeline, program data, staff and alumni voices
- **Cinematic documentary** -- The Buttery's 50-year cinematic documentary, already in build, screening at capital campaign launch event

> A caravan as a venue, a dignity infrastructure prototype, and an art piece all at once. Born out of the Community Capital Leadership Retreat.

## Overview

The Caravan is an ACT studio piece that emerged from the **10x10 Community Capital Leadership Retreat** in Bowral (February 2026, see [[community-capital|Community Capital]]). It sits in the lineage of [[feel-good-project|Feel Good Project]] and [[global-laundry-alliance|Orange Sky's mobile dignity model]] — vehicles that turn up where the people are, instead of asking the people to come to them.

But it's also an art piece in the [[act-ecosystem|Studio cluster]] sense: the caravan is a thing that carries an argument. The argument is that infrastructure for community capital — leadership retreats, peer councils, dignity services — shouldn't live in conference rooms in capital cities. It should be towable.

## Origin: the Community Capital event

The Community Capital Leadership Retreat (Bowral, Feb 2026, funded by Social Impact Hub Foundation) brought ten community leaders together. The Caravan was the contribution ACT made to that event — both as a literal vehicle and as a statement about what happens when you invert "we built a building, come to us" into "we built a thing, we're coming to you."

[[nicholas-marchesi|Nicholas Marchesi]]'s Orange Sky pattern is the obvious precedent: a van turning up in a park is a more powerful equity intervention than a brochure. The Caravan extends that logic to leadership development.

## Status

Evidence sparse on specifics — exact build details, current location, future tour stops, and post-Bowral activations all await deeper source ingestion. This article is the seed.

## Connections

- Born at: [[community-capital|Community Capital — 10x10 Leadership Retreat]]
- Pattern lineage: [[feel-good-project|Feel Good Project]] (mobile beauty), [[global-laundry-alliance|Global Laundry Alliance]] (mobile laundry), [[gold-phone|Gold.Phone]] (mobile communication)
- ACT's [[act-ecosystem|Studio cluster]]
- Embodies [[beautiful-obsolescence|beautiful obsolescence]] — designed to be handed over to whoever needs it next

## Studio Context

The Caravan matters because it shows the Studio line is not only about gallery objects. It is also about mobile infrastructure, hosted presence, and practical dignity that can move between communities. It belongs with [[art-projects|ACT Art Projects]], [[art/innovation/studio-innovation-flow|Studio Innovation Flow]], and [[art/business/studio-business-model|Studio Business Model]] as one of the works where ACT's art, strategy, and service logic overlap.

## LCAA Phase

In the [[lcaa-method|LCAA Method]], The Caravan sits across **Action** and **Art** — the wiki backlink already names it: *"Action and Art in one object."* It is a literal vehicle that carries leadership development infrastructure to the people, instead of asking the people to come to a conference room in a capital city.

LCAA arc for The Caravan:
- **Listen** — the [[community-capital|10x10 Community Capital Leadership Retreat]] in Bowral was the listening room; The Caravan is the artefact that carried what was heard outward
- **Curiosity** — what happens when you invert *"we built a building, come to us"* into *"we built a thing, we're coming to you"*? The same logic that made Orange Sky's vans more powerful than a brochure
- **Action** — built infrastructure: a vehicle that exists, a venue that travels; resident at [[black-cockatoo-valley|Black Cockatoo Valley]] and available for future Community Capital convenings
- **Art** — a thing that carries an argument; the caravan as both dignity-infrastructure prototype and Studio piece, embodying [[beautiful-obsolescence|beautiful obsolescence]] — designed to be handed over to whoever needs it next

The Caravan extends the [[feel-good-project|Feel Good Project]] / [[global-laundry-alliance|Orange Sky]] mobile-dignity grammar from service delivery into leadership development.

pages.title: The Caravan at BCV
pages.excerpt: The Caravan was built for the Community Capital retreat in Bowral. It now lives at Black Cockatoo Valley. A mobile dignity object, parked on Country, still working. This is the case study of what happens when a studio piece stops touring and takes up residence.
pages.content:
> The Caravan was built for the Community Capital retreat in Bowral. It now lives at Black Cockatoo Valley. A mobile dignity object, parked on Country, still working. This is the case study of what happens when a studio piece stops touring and takes up residence.

**Status:** Published | **Code:** ACT-FM-CS-the-caravan-at-bcv | **Cluster:** [[act-farm|ACT Farm]]

## Snapshot

| Item | Detail |
|------|--------|
| **When** | Built for Bowral, 23–25 Feb 2025; resident at BCV from 2026, 12-month arrangement |
| **Where** | [[black-cockatoo-valley|Black Cockatoo Valley]], Jinibara Country |
| **Who** | ACT studio build; funded via [[community-capital|Community Capital]]; hosted by ACT Farm |
| **Related experience** | [[experiences/the-space-at-bcv|The Space at BCV]] |
| **Sibling case studies** | [[case-studies/community-capital-at-bcv|Community Capital at BCV]] · [[case-studies/community-capital-bowral-2025|Community Capital — Bowral, 23–25 Feb 2025]] |
| **Notional rate** | $550/month, unbilled |

## What happened

[[the-caravan|The Caravan]] emerged from the 10x10 Community Capital Leadership Retreat in Bowral (Phase 1, 23–25 February 2025). It was part of the contribution ACT made to that event — both a literal vehicle and a statement: infrastructure for community capital shouldn't live in conference rooms in capital cities, it should be towable.

After Bowral, the Caravan came to BCV. It has been here since, parked and hosted at a notional $550/month that isn't being billed. The original touring logic — turn up where the people are, like [[global-laundry-alliance|Orange Sky's]] vans, like the [[feel-good-project|Feel Good Project]] — now runs alongside a second logic: sometimes the most useful move is to stay put, become part of a place, and let people come to it.

## What we did

- **We built a caravan that carries an argument.** Leadership development, capital convening, and community dignity services don't have to be office-bound. A caravan says that out loud.
- **We deployed it at Bowral.** The Caravan was part of the Phase 1 retreat infrastructure — present, used, photographed, felt.
- **We brought it home to BCV.** Instead of warehousing it or running it as a full tour between convenings, we installed it at Black Cockatoo Valley for a 12-month residency. It sits on Country now. Community Capital convenings that come to BCV can use it. So can visiting artists, storytelling residencies, and groups hiring the convening space.
- **We held it at zero billed cost** for the 12-month period. ACT carries the nominal $550/month; Community Capital funded its build and its Phase 1 use. The Caravan is paid forward into the ecosystem, not rented out.

## What the work produced

**A studio object that crossed registers.** The Caravan is art (it makes an argument), infrastructure (it hosts conversations), and case study (it's now evidence of what ACT studio practice produces). Most studio pieces settle in one of those registers. The Caravan stays in all three.

**A reusable dignity-infrastructure pattern.** The Caravan, the [[feel-good-project|Feel Good Project]], [[global-laundry-alliance|Global Laundry Alliance]], and [[gold-phone|Gold.Phone]] are now a named lineage: *mobile dignity infrastructure*. The pattern travels; the specific object at BCV is one instance of it.

**An anchor for the BCV convening offer.** Groups that hire [[experiences/the-space-at-bcv|The Space at BCV]] can choose to work with the Caravan as part of their convening. It's a gathering object that changes the shape of a conversation — small, enclosed, equal-footed — in a way a room can't.

**A living example of [[designing-for-obsolescence|beautiful obsolescence]].** The Caravan is designed to be handed over to whoever needs it next. The BCV residency is a way-station in that life, not a final destination.

## What we learned

- **Studio objects can have second careers.** The Caravan's first career was the Bowral retreat. Its second is BCV residency. Treating a studio piece as a one-shot is a category mistake — the object keeps working if we keep placing it.
- **Towable and rooted are not opposites.** The argument the Caravan makes (infrastructure should come to people) is not contradicted by it living on Country for a year. That residency is itself a form of placement.
- **Unbilled hosting is a form of investment.** Carrying $550/month in unbilled accommodation is ACT investing in the longevity of the object and the program, not a favour to Community Capital. It compounds.

## Evidence

- [[the-caravan|The Caravan]] canonical wiki page — the studio-cluster seed article
- INV-0289 — line-items the caravan reno cost from Phase 1 build (see [[case-studies/community-capital-bowral-2025|Bowral case study]])
